**Request: Reevaluate JavaScript Array Indexing and Length Conversion**

We propose revisiting the behavior of JavaScript arrays regarding index and length conversions in ES6 and beyond. Currently, array indices and lengths are coerced to 32-bit unsigned integers ( ToUint32 ), causing negative values between -2^31 and -1 to be treated as positive values in the range 2^31 to 2^32-1.

In contrast, we propose applying a simpler ToInteger conversion in these array-related places. This change would prevent unwrapping of negative values into large positive values and may enable larger arrays than currently possible.

The goal is to test whether this change will not break existing web applications before committing to it. The hypothesis is that the uint32 conversions have little practical utility for arrays, making this change unlikely to cause issues. However, we need to verify this on actual web content before proceeding.

This change would affect basic array property accesses and all array methods, even when used with non-array objects, as well as specific cases like ''.split and Function.prototype.apply.

summary: preconnect http sessions before cache lookup
description:
As discussed at the work week, this patch implements a necko-specific speculative-connect API for use when we think a connection to a particular host will be needed "soon".

It also adds code to do this preconnect very early in the HTTP path - before the cache is consulted. That way any latency added by the cache can overlap with the connection establishment.

The connection is driven through any TCP or SSL handshakes. A "null transaction" is introduced to do the SSL portion if necessary. It is not necessary if we're not using SSL (duh) or if by the time the TCP portion of the transaction is setup there is a real transaction in the pending queue.

Currently the only case of connections that aren't paired with transactions are leftover cases from syn-retry timers firing. Currently those only do TCP handshake, but this patch extends them to do the SSL handshake as well if apropos.

An implementation side effect of this is that we do NPN for all SSL now, though if spdy is disabled we don't put spdy in the list of acceptable choices. This is because NPN is part of the path used to drive SSL when there is no transaction data to send. While its not strictly required, in practice this isn't much of a change as spdy by default is the direction we are heading and it can be argued that npn all-the-time is desirable anyhow.

my measured savings aren't impressive - but I can never reproduce any of the cache problems other people have seen. so I expect this would extend significant gains to them. Typically I see latency improvements of 2 or 3 ms, with the most extreme being 8.

Taras, you might want to measure as part of snappy?

The next step will be an hint-based idl for use by non necko things. I'll block 723628 on that work. The ability for a click in the search box to initiate a handshake has big potential imo. (especially when we get rid of the painful http->https redirection from bug 633773)

**Title:** Preconnect HTTP Sessions Prior to Cache Lookup

**Description:**

We propose implementing an early preconnection mechanism for HTTP sessions using the necko-specific speculative-connect API. This feature aims to mitigate latency by initiating connections with targeted hosts before cache lookup, allowing any subsequent cache access latency to overlap with connection establishment.

The solution involves driving TCP or SSL handshakes through a "null transaction" when necessary, ensuring that only required connections are established. The implementation also extends the existing syn-retry timer functionality to include SSL handshakes for unpaired connections.

As an additional benefit, this patch enables Network Protocol Negotiation (NPN) for all SSL sessions by default, with the exception of cases where SPDY is disabled. This change aligns with the current development direction and allows for potential performance improvements in scenarios where cache issues arise.

**Expected Benefits:**

The proposed solution is expected to provide significant latency reductions, with observed improvements ranging from 2-8 milliseconds under various workloads. We anticipate that this enhancement will yield substantial benefits for users experiencing cache-related performance issues.

**Next Steps:**

Future development will focus on introducing a hint-based IDL (Interface Definition Language) for non-necko components, enabling them to initiate preconnections and further optimize HTTP session establishment. This effort is expected to complement the existing work on improving HTTP performance, as described in bug 723628.

**Request:** Allocate nsFrameLists from Pres Shell Arena for Memory Efficiency and Leak Detection

**Purpose:** Reconsider memory allocation strategy for nsFrameLists to improve efficiency and reduce potential leaks.

**Details:**

* Currently, allocating heap nsFrameLists requires individual memory management, which may lead to fragmentation and inefficient memory use.
* Allocating these lists from the pres shell arena would:
	+ Utilize the LRU cache, potentially improving performance.
	+ Avoid separate memory deallocation for each list when destroying the shell.
	+ Enable leak detection by default upon pres shell destruction.

**Considerations:**

* Potential benefits of using PresArena's poisoning feature are mitigated by the fact that nsFrameList members are already poisoned.
* The proposed FramePropertyTable changes for destructor support may be unnecessary and could be replaced with manual memory management in the respective owning frames.

Here is a standardized description of the enhancement request:

**Title:** Experiment with Variable Ping Keep-Alive Values in SPDY

**Description:**

We propose an experiment to gather data on optimal keep-alive values for SPDY connections. Currently, we use a fixed value based on idle time (around 60 seconds), but our research indicates that lower NAT timeout values may exist (e.g., 44 seconds). To determine the most effective threshold, we will randomly assign a custom ping timer to a subset of SPDY sessions with telemetry enabled.

**Implementation:**

* For approximately 1 in 1500 SPDY sessions using telemetry, a random ping threshold between 10 and 180 seconds (default configuration) will be assigned.
* When the ping timer fires, we will report via telemetry whether a timeout was detected and the corresponding timer value. A timeout indicates that the chosen value was too large.

**Goals:**

This experiment aims to provide data-driven insights into the optimal keep-alive values for SPDY connections, which will inform future configuration decisions. The results have implications beyond SPDY, as they can be applied to HTTP as well. However, since HTTP lacks a comparable ping mechanism, it cannot measure these parameters in the same way.

**Background:**

Our research has identified potential lower NAT timeout values (e.g., 60 seconds) that warrant investigation. This experiment leverages existing telemetry data, ensuring no additional site tracking is required to gather insights into client topology and optimal keep-alive settings.

summary: Handle CSS transforms of fixed backgrounds per spec
description:
Spec bug: https://www.w3.org/Bugs/Public/show_bug.cgi?id=15833

The spec now says:

"""
Fixed backgrounds are affected by any transform specified for the root element, and not by any other transforms.

Note: Thus an element with a fixed background still acts like a "porthole" into an image that's fixed to the viewport, and transforms on the element affect the porthole, not the background behind it. On the other hand, transforming the root element will still transform everything on the page, rather than everything except for fixed backgrounds.
"""

This is not anything like what Gecko does.  Other browsers all do other things.  If the spec should say something different, I'm happy to change it; otherwise Gecko should change to match the spec.

There are several reftests I wrote for the W3C test suite that could be reused here: <http://hg.csswg.org/test/rev/41a7369b5bf3>.  Gecko fails almost all of them.

summary: Limit or remove OS information in User-Agent
description:
As documented by Peter Eckersley (link below), the User Agent header can be used as an aide in uniquely identifying an individual or computer (Peter estimates that on average about 1/1500 people have the same agent as you).

One aspect that helps make the User Agent unique is the OS component, which contains not only the type of OS (Linux, Windows, Mac) but also the version being run.

Some examples are:
    (Windows; U; Windows NT 5.1; en-US; rv:1.9.1.3)
    (Macintosh; U; Intel Mac OS X 10.5; en-US; rv:1.9.1.3)
    (X11; U; Linux i686; en-US; rv:1.9.0.14) Gecko/2009090216 Ubuntu/9.04 (jaunty)

I propose that an option be added to restrict or eliminate OS information included in the User Agent header. By reducing entropy contained in the header, user privacy can be enhanced!

UI options could include a checkbox on the Privacy tab entitled "Send system information to websites I visit" or perhaps a cascading set of options with one called "Send Operating System type to sites I visit" and a conditional one called "Send Operating System version to sites".

The only downside I can think of would be software download sites which customize download pages depending on the user's OS. These sites could still potentially use javascript. An interesting corollary to this request would be to similarly restrict OS information via javascript.

Respectfully Yours,
Jay

User Agent tracking: https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2010/01/tracking-by-user-agent
Panopticlick: https://panopticlick.eff.org/

**Purpose:** Provide a mechanism to notify the application of changes to the scrollable overflow area, enabling timely updates to the display-port dimensions.

summary: Include redirection count in request headers to help redirect loop detection
description:
Server bugs resulting in infinite redirect loops can be hard for the maintainer of the server to detect: since the redirect happens as soon as the response headers are received, Javascript etc. is not available, and the server can only use cookies (and sessions) to keep track of redirects. Cookies are shared between browser tabs and windows, so if the user has many tabs and/or the tabs issue lots of AJAX requests, a cookie- or session-based redirect counter could behave in unpredictable ways.

A simple solution to this problem is to send the redirect count as a HTTP header:
- if the HTTP request sent by the browser is a follow-up to a HTTP 30x response, the redirect count is one plus the redirect count of the request belonging to that response;
- otherwise the redirect count is zero;
- if the redirect count is non-zero, include an "X-Redirect-Count: <redirect count>" header in the request.
That way, the server could detect if the redirect count goes e.g. over 10, and log an error. Right now, this kind of error usually goes unnoticed.

Another possible solution would be to implement an auto-notification scheme, something like Content Security Policy violation reports.

To improve the installation process for Browserscope tests, we propose replacing the current tar/untar approach with `nsinstall`. This modification aims to address two main issues:

summary: Parse <font size> per HTML5
description:
Our current algorithm for parsing <font size> is something like:

1) Strip whitespace from start and end.
2) If the string begins with "+" or "-":
  a) Truncate the string at the first non-digit character after the first.
  b) If the remaining string is exactly one of "-10", "-9", ..., "-0", "+0", "+1", ..., "+10", then add three and clamp to [1, 7].
  c) Otherwise, parse error.
3) Otherwise, parse as an integer, dropping any trailing non-digit characters.

HTML5 says what to do here:

http://www.whatwg.org/specs/web-apps/current-work/multipage/rendering.html#phrasing-content-1

It's almost the same, except that it will accept any integer with a plus or minus sign, not just -10 to +10.  So it treats +11 the same as +10.  This makes more sense than what Gecko currently does.

summary: Throw an error or warning when a unsafe https resource is being blocked.
description:
User Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux i686) AppleWebKit/535.19 (KHTML, like Gecko) Ubuntu/11.10 Chromium/18.0.1025.151 Chrome/18.0.1025.151 Safari/535.19

Steps to reproduce:

We created a web application for high schools and are hosting it on our CA certified HTTPS host. The web application also has some embedded resources from other HTTPS sites. It embed some js / css files from these hosts: 

https://maps.gstatic.com
https://www.google.com
https://maps.google.com
https://maps.googleapis.com


Actual results:

Teachers and students reported that the website was not working on some computers in some schools. It was working on some other computers. It was very strange and took very long to debug.

It turned out that the schools are using an internal proxy server that filters all HTTP and HTTPS traffic. They do this to prevent students from opening adult sites. However, as a side effect all of the HTTPS requests encrypted with a self-signed certificate on the proxy instead of the actual certificate from the host. 

As a result, for every https site that students open in the browser they get to see the 'unsafe ssl certificate' warning and have to confirm the security exception. I think this is really bad policy from the school, but unfortunately that is out of my control.

However, the reason the sites were not working was because of the embedded https resources from other domains. These were all silently blocked. Instead of issuing a warning that the web application was trying to load content from a host with an self-signed certificate, it would just not do anything.


Expected results:

Whenever firefox blocks an embedded https resource because the ssl certificate is untrusted, it should throw a warning or error. Something to let the developer know.

If you directly open a https website that has an untrusted certificate, you get to see the big warning and you have an option to make a security exception. **Reported Issue:**

When attempting to load HTTPS resources with self-signed certificates via embedded links or AJAX calls, the browser should display an error or warning notification to inform developers of potential issues.

The browser should display an error or warning message when attempting to load embedded HTTPS resources with self-signed certificates, alerting developers to potential issues and facilitating easier troubleshooting.

**Request to Consolidate Action Enums**

The current action enum definitions for `nsEditor`, `nsHTMLEditor`, and an anonymous text edit rules enum exhibit inconsistencies, overlapping values, and lack of type safety. Specifically:

* Duplicate values exist between enums (e.g., 1000: `kUndo`/`kOpInsertBreak`, 1001: `kRedo`/`kOpInsertText`)
* Enum values from different domains overlap or conflict (e.g., `nsEditor::kOpInsertBreak` vs. `nsHTMLEditor::kOpInsertBreak`)
* The anonymous text edit rules enum contains a mix of actions with no clear organization

To address these issues, it is proposed to consolidate these action enums into a single, well-organized enum that ensures:

* Unique and distinct values for each action
* Clear categorization and naming conventions across different domains
* Improved type safety by using a unified data type (e.g., `PRInt32`)

This consolidation would simplify the handling of actions, reduce potential bugs due to value conflicts, and enhance overall maintainability.

**Feature Request: Support for Strongly-Typed Enumerations (C++11)**

We propose implementing support for strongly-typed enumerations, also known as enumeration classes, as specified in the C++11 standard. This feature would enable developers to define enums with scoped values, preventing unintentional type conversions and promoting code robustness.

**Benefits:**

* Improved error detection and prevention of silent type conversions
* Enhanced code maintainability and readability through explicit scoping
* Consistency with emerging industry standards (GCC support since 4.4, VC implementation underway)

**Implementation Considerations:**

* Fallback mechanism for legacy code or platforms without C++11 support
* Potential scoping implications and impact on existing codebases

This feature is recommended as a wishlist enhancement to improve the overall quality and reliability of our codebase.

The current error message for NS_ERROR_XPC_JSOBJECT_HAS_NO_FUNCTION_NAMED is ambiguous and requires clarification. (Unlike Dropbox which also stores the keys on the server). Currently such services are not practical, because in addition to platform-specific and mobile software implementations, users usually want to have a web interface as well.

**Request:** Implement Support for "http+aes" Scheme

**Description:**

We propose implementing the "http+aes" scheme, as defined by the WHATWG specification (March 2012). This scheme enables secure data transfer between client and server by encrypting HTTP requests with AES encryption.

The primary goal of this implementation is to support storage services that deliver encrypted files directly in a web interface. This will facilitate the creation of cloud-based services that provide full encryption on the server-side, only decrypting data on the client-side. This approach improves security by reducing the risk of key exposure and allows for more secure client-side encryption.

Although some may argue that "http+aes" does not ensure secure client-side encryption due to potential vulnerabilities in web interface scripting, this implementation will still provide a significant improvement over current solutions. For users accessing storage services through a web interface, this scheme will offer enhanced protection against data breaches.

To further enhance security, browser extensions can be developed to monitor scripts from these sites and detect potential changes or backdoors.

**Benefits:**

* Improved security for users accessing storage services through a web interface
* Reduced risk of key exposure and data breaches
* Support for cloud-based services that provide full encryption on the server-side

summary: Get rid of useless nsresult in editor/
description:
After discussion in bug 757371 comment 8 ff., I poked around at nsresult usage in editor that could be easily removed.  There's not as much as I'd hoped, but still quite a bit.

One major category of nontrivial nsresult usage is stuff that QI's to nsINode or nsIContent and does NS_ENSURE_TRUE; that will go away as more functions are ported to use those types directly.  Likewise things use nsIDOMNode methods like GetChildNodes() that return nsresult, where the corresponding nsIContent etc. methods always succeed.

The difficult thing is when errors are being returned because the function actually can't do anything sensible.  A selection that has no ranges or that has an endpoint in a weird place (like a Document) is a very common scenario that needs to be handled.  I don't think returning nsresult is the right thing to do there, but I'm not sure what is.

I'm about to attach a patch, which removes nsresult from functions in the following cases:

* A surprising number of methods returned NS_OK unconditionally but still returned nsresult.
* Some did null pointer checks, which I changed to MOZ_ASSERT.  We seem to be okay with doing that, right?  (I'm not actually sure why.)
* nsWSRunObject::GetRuns() does a lot of NS_ENSURE_TRUE after "new WSFragment()".  I was told that that might be infallible already, and if it's not it should be soon.  Anyway, MOZ_ASSERT is certainly fine here.
* nsWSRunObject::GetChar(Before|After) did NS_ENSURE_TRUE on an array element after doing explicit bounds-checking that should make it impossible for it to be null (unless the array can actually have null pointers inserted into it?).  Changed to MOZ_ASSERT.

Sadly, this doesn't make a real dent in nsresult use.  I was hoping that once I removed nsresult from enough easy methods, their callers could stop using it too, but too make things trace back to things like QI to nsIContent that can't be removed quite this trivially.

summary: GC: Add new GC zeal modes to exercise incremental collection
description:
Currently it's difficult to test incremental collection because it doesn't always happen that often.  We can improve this by adding some new GC zeal modes, which would periodically trigger on allocation.  These would:

 1. Do only root marking in the first slice (as if the budget is zero) and then finish the GC in the second slice.

 2. Do all marking in the first slice and then leave before doing any sweeping. In the second slice, do any new marking work that write barriers might have created and then finish the GC.

 3. Run multiple slices, limiting the collection to X objects where X is doubled every slice until all objects have been marked.

standard:
Here is a standardized description of the enhancement request:

**Request:** Enhance Garbage Collection (GC) Zeal Modes for Incremental Collection Testing

**Description:**

To facilitate more effective testing and debugging of incremental garbage collection, we propose introducing three new GC zeal modes that can be triggered periodically based on allocation events. These modes will enable more controlled and repeatable scenarios for testing incremental collection.

**Proposed Features:**

1. **Root Marking Only**: The first slice will perform root marking as if the budget were zero, followed by completion of the GC in the second slice.
2. **Partial Sweeping**: The first slice will mark all objects, but sweeping will be skipped. In the second slice, any new marking work created by write barriers will be performed, and then the GC will be completed.
3. **Tiered Collection**: Multiple slices will be implemented, limiting collection to a specific number of objects (X) that doubles in each subsequent slice until all objects have been marked.

These enhancements aim to improve our ability to test and validate incremental garbage collection behavior under various conditions.

* Potential refcounting requirements for the nsIURI argument
* Compatibility with other channel types

The existing patch demonstrates effective functionality, addressing a URL spoofing bug and offering a viable alternative to NoScript's ChannelReplacement.js. Further refinement of the implementation is necessary to ensure proper integration and address any edge cases.

**Request Summary**

Modify the implementation of `NS_SUCCEEDED` and `NS_FAILED` macros in C++ to use inline functions instead of macro expansions. This change will improve code readability by eliminating complex macro expansions.

**Current Implementation**

The current implementation uses a combination of macros and inline functions, depending on the presence of `NS_STATIC_CHECKING` and the C++ compiler being used. However, this leads to cumbersome macro expansions that can make debugging assertions difficult to read.

**Proposed Change**

Remove the conditionals related to `NS_STATIC_CHECKING` and use inline functions for `NS_SUCCEEDED` and `NS_FAILED` in all C++ code. This will simplify the implementation and improve code readability.

**Rationale**

This change is driven by the desire to avoid complex macro expansions, which can obscure the meaning of assertions like the one shown in bug 767169. By using inline functions instead, developers will be able to more easily understand and debug their code.

**Portability Considerations**

The proposal includes a question about whether to retain the `#if defined(__cplusplus)` conditional or allow C compilers to use inline functions as well. Further investigation is needed to determine the best course of action for ensuring compatibility with all relevant compilers.

summary: Try "include-what-you-use" on editor/
description:
See bug 634839.  In theory, it might cut down on compile times.  In practice, it seems buggy and it didn't create a big improvement for me.  It got down compilation of editor/ on a hot cache with ccache cleared from maybe 26s to 25s.  On the other hand, it's possible that it will reduce incremental compile times by removing unnecessary dependencies.  And it alphabetizes #includes, which is a nice bonus!  And adds comments saying what the files are used for.

For a lot of files it only adds includes, for things that are otherwise only indirectly included.  But for instance, in nsEditor.h it converts a lot of includes to forward declarations -- it figured out that things like nsIContent.h didn't have to be included.  It got nsHTMLCSSUtils.h down to four includes -- nsCOMPtr, nsTArray, prtypes, and nscore.

Sometimes I don't know what it thinks it's doing -- like including nsAString.h, nsString.h, and nsStringFwd.h in the same file.  But that doesn't hurt anything, I guess.

I had to patiently teach it not to include stuff like string-template-def-char.h, but I think I mostly succeeded.

The command I'm using is this, having gotten SVN checkouts as described in bug 634839:

find editor -type f -exec touch {} + && make -k -j16 -C objdir-ff-release/editor/libeditor/base CXX=/tmp/llvm/Release+Asserts/bin/include-what-you-use 2>&1 | tee /tmp/iwyu.out | python /tmp/llvm/tools/clang/tools/include-what-you-use/fix_includes.py --nosafe_headers --comments

I go directory-by-directory because it tends to die.  I have to do manual fixups after that, mostly due to <http://code.google.com/p/include-what-you-use/issues/detail?id=74>.

So in conclusion, this was interesting and doesn't hurt anything, but in retrospect, probably was not worth the time.  :/

summary: Always BindAttribLocation something to attrib 0 if possible
description:
Currently on all desktop GL platforms, there's a performance penalty when vertex attrib zero is not an enabled vertex attrib array. This can be for two reasons:

1:
The GLSL linker set an attrib's location to 0 when it is not an attrib array. (vertexAttrib[1234]f{v} instead of vertexAttribPointer)

2:
The GLSL linker did not assign an attrib to location 0.

We should try to assign *something* to attrib 0, in hopes that we can bind a vertex attrib array to 0.

Note that we won't be able to do anything if someone binds all their attribs to non-zero locations. We can't change the user's binding choices without breaking things, but we *can* try to prevent the linker from doing something silly.

Further, we could incorporate a heuristic where we try to check if one of the attribs is the vertex position attribute, which should always be an array. We can try to check if one of the attribs has a name containing 'position' or 'pos', and try binding that to 0. (if possible)

**Description:**

To mitigate performance penalties on desktop GL platforms, we propose modifying the vertex attribute binding behavior to assign an attribute to location 0 whenever possible. This approach aims to take advantage of the GLSL linker's default behavior when no vertex attribute array is specified.

**Purpose:** Improve the efficiency of atom collection by reducing unnecessary sweeping and marking operations.

At present, finalization of things that can be finalized on the background thread may happen at a different time relative to other parts of sweeping depending on whether they are in fact finalized in the background.

This is undesirable because the sweeping code must handle both possibilites, but one is only rarely exercised.

The proposed solution is to finalize these objects at the same point in collection regardless of which thread they are being finalized from, and to unify the code path as much as possible.

summary: Use multiple host addresses when available
description: When multiple addresses, i.e. A or AAAA records, exist for a host name, the browser should, for increased availability and speed, a) attempt to open connections to all (or at most e.g. 5) addresses concurrently b) start the HTTP-requests on the best connection. For the first request the best connection is probably the one that connects first, but for subsequent requests availability, latency and bandwidth (e.g. if one address is much slower than the others, don't use it even if it is idle) can be considered. Statistics can probably be kept for addresses independent of host name. c) restart stalled requests on other connections (e.g. using a range request to pickup). The stalled request might be canceled after the new request is verified to be better. d) for requests with a content-length over some limit (and perhaps only if a e-tag and/or a last-modified header also exist) use range requests to download multiple parts of the file simultaneously. (c) and (d) can probably be combined by using the estimated time remaining as the criteria instead of the content-length. As an example, suppose you setup two a-records for the domain *.a.example.com to point to two webservers, both serving that wildcard-domian and both with an image at the address /a.gif, one server serving up a blue and one a green image. There multiple host names is pointed to the same address to get more simultaneous downloads from the same host. This bug tries to address the problem where some hosts are unavailable, slow or far away, which sites might try to mitigate using fail-over (using load balancers, dns or bgp-routing) and geolocation-aware dns. Here is a standardized description based on the enhancement request:

**Request:** Implement Concurrent Connection and Failover for Multiple Host Addresses

**Description:**

To enhance availability and speed, the browser should utilize multiple host addresses when available. When multiple A or AAAA records exist for a host name, the browser will attempt to establish connections to all (or up to 5) addresses concurrently. The best connection will be used to initiate HTTP requests, taking into consideration factors such as availability, latency, and bandwidth.

For subsequent requests, the browser will continue to use the best available connection based on real-time statistics. Stalled requests will be restarted on other connections using range requests when necessary. Additionally, for large file downloads with a content length exceeding a specified threshold (and in conjunction with an E-tag or Last-Modified header), the browser will utilize range requests to download multiple parts of the file simultaneously.

This enhancement will enable seamless failover between connections and reduce the impact of slow or unavailable hosts on page loading performance. The proposed implementation will also ensure that clients can access content even if some host addresses are not reachable, such as IPv4-only devices accessing IPv6-enabled servers.

**Request:** Implement Void Versions of NS_ENSURE_* Macros

**Description:** The build process for the Firefox source code fails when attempting to compile using both GCC (version 4.4.5) and Clang due to unresolved issues with certain macros. To resolve this issue, we propose implementing void versions of the NS_ENSURE_* macros to prevent crashes or unexpected exit codes during compilation.

**Solution:** By introducing void versions of the NS_ENSURE_* macros, we can prevent compilation errors and ensure a successful build process for the Firefox source code on the specified platform.

summary: GC: Sweep compartments in groups
description:
The sweeping phase of GC involves a bunch of processing that has to happen for all collecting compartments as they transition from being marked to being swept, before returning to the caller.  This work cannot be performed incrementally and therefore can lead to noticeable pauses when many compartments are being collected.

One way round this is to not transition all compartments from marking to sweeping in one go.  There are however dependencies between compartments that mean there are constraints on the order compartments can be swept in, and that some compartments must be swept at the same time.

Specifically, if there pointer from an unmarked object in compartment A to unmarked object in compartment B then compartment B must not be swept before A.  If the these pointers are considered as edges in a graph, then the components that must be swept at the same time are the strongly connected components of the graph.

A configuration option should be added to about:config to let the user selectively disable a CSP for particular URIs, without the need to disable CSP at all.


Background:
I tried to execute a userscript via Greasemonkey to add MathJax [1] to a particular site with CSP enabled [2], that means adding the capability to render math equations inside this site. Having said this, I would like to advocate for a more granular possibility to disable CSP only for particular URIs, e.g. by adding a new option `security.csp.disabledURLs` to about:config. I think this enhancement will be in harmony with Mozilla's Principles [3], especially with No. 5 "Individuals must have the ability to shape their own experiences on the Internet." and as such it would be valuable for all users.

**Enhancement Request:** Granular CSP Disabling for Specific URIs

**Description:**

A new configuration option, `security.csp.disabledURLs`, is proposed to be added to about:config. This feature would enable users to selectively disable Content Security Policy (CSP) for specific Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs), allowing for a more granular control over CSP settings.

**Background:**

This request aligns with Mozilla's core principles, particularly the emphasis on user autonomy and customization.

**Request:**

Add a new about:config preference `security.csp.disabledURLs` that allows users to specify individual URIs or domains where CSP should be disabled. This feature would enhance user experience by providing more flexibility in balancing security concerns with specific use cases.

**Title:** Evaluate Disk Cache Performance Against HTTP Conditional Revalidations

**Description:** We aim to investigate and optimize the performance of our system by racing disk cache access times against HTTP conditional revalidation. To achieve this, we will create a prototype to measure the latency associated with accessing cached resources versus those requiring conditional validation.

**Key Objectives:**

1. Store ETag/LM information in memory cache to enable efficient conditional validations.
2. Implement mechanisms to minimize queueing of non-conditional requests due to excessive conditional revalidations.

**Rationale:** This exercise will help us understand the performance implications of our current caching setup and inform decisions regarding cache size optimizations or alternative caching strategies.

**Target Environment:** Perform measurements using Stone Ridge to evaluate system performance under various loads.

description:
I hope to make channel priorities a more useful attribute in necko so I'm cleaning up the priority some resource requests are classified with.

OCSP and CRL are both currently executed with default priority.

Neither of these changes will have an immediate impact because current prioritization only happens among resources with the same hostname; this is about better meta data to allow experimentation/measurement with other approaches.

summary: Ability for XMLHTTPRequest to automatically encode request body
description:
A common pattern when using XHR is to apply some kind of encoding to the request body. Compression is probably the most likely one.

I think it would be rad if Mozilla's XHR type had a non-standard property or something that would allow seamless encoding of request data. No nsIStreamConverterService or similar XPCOM voodoo. Just set a property or call a method and let XHR do all the work behind the scenes.

For example:

  let request = Cc["@mozilla.org/xmlextra/xmlhttprequest;1"]
                  .createInstance(Ci.nsIXMLHttpRequest);

  request.mozCompression = "gzip"; // Sets Content-Encoding: gzip
  request.open("POST", url, true);
  request.send(my_big_blob_of_raw_data); // Payload is automagically compressed with gzip

Since Content-Encoding can be stacked, perhaps we could expose a simple API for registering encoders and decoders:

  request.pushEncoder("base64");
  request.pushEncoder("compress");

This would result in "Content-Encoding: base64, compress". That's arguably not very useful, but you get the idea.

I'd argue that such a feature should be on XHR itself because Content-Encoding, like Transfer-Encoding, is likely a feature baked into HTTP agents themselves. XHR already transparently decodes Content-Encoding on responses. I think it should have the ability to do it on requests as well.

Are the Necko people receptive to this idea? Again, I'm only proposing a Mozilla-specific extension. And, I'm most interested in having it from Gecko - if people don't want to expose this to content because it is non-standard, I'm OK with that.

Here is a standardized description of the enhancement request:

**Request: Automatic Encoding for XMLHttpRequest Request Body**

We propose adding an extension to the Mozilla's XMLHttpRequest (XHR) type to enable automatic encoding of the request body. This feature would allow developers to seamlessly encode request data using various algorithms, such as compression or base64 encoding, without requiring additional XPCOM services.

The proposed implementation includes setting a non-standard property or calling a method to enable encoding. For example:

* Setting a `mozCompression` property with a specific algorithm, e.g., "gzip".
* Exposing an API for registering encoders and decoders, allowing multiple algorithms to be stacked.

This enhancement would mirror the behavior of Content-Encoding on responses, which is already handled by XHR. The feature would be useful for content developers who need to compress or encode large amounts of data in their requests.

We are interested in exploring this idea with the Necko team and discuss potential implementation details. This proposal focuses on a Mozilla-specific extension, and we acknowledge that exposing it to content may require careful consideration due to its non-standard nature.

summary: SpiderMonkey should stop trying to recover from most OOM
description:
* What little testing of OOM handling we've done has shown that many paths in the JS engine do not recover correctly.  A significant fraction of these bugs affect memory safety.  (See bug 471528, bug 687256, and bug 624094.)

* Most of the browser (along with some pieces of SpiderMonkey, such as YARR and the IonMonkey compiler) do not attempt to recover from small-allocation failures.  So when Firefox is out of memory, it's probably going to crash eventually anyway.

* Chrome JS is impossible to analyze if a web page can cause its execution to just halt, at any point, by leaving just the right amount of memory available.

I think SpiderMonkey should

- Try to recover in a few cases (strings and arrays)
  - Perhaps with the rule that it must be an exception rather than a terminate()
  - But notify the embedding, so it can bail if security-relevant chrome JS OOMs

- Avoid starting big computations (e.g. parsing or compiling) when low on memory

- Just crash on OOM "by default" and wherever it's not obvious how to recover

Here is a standardized description of the enhancement request:

**Request:** Enhance SpiderMonkey's Out-of-Memory (OOM) Handling

**Purpose:** Improve SpiderMonkey's resilience when encountering low memory conditions, prioritizing memory safety while allowing for controlled recovery in specific cases.

**Details:**

1. **Recovery in Limited Cases**: Implement OOM recovery mechanisms for certain data structures, such as strings and arrays, with the exception of critical operations like termination.
2. **Notify Embedding of OOM Events**: Provide notifications to the embedding environment when an OOM occurs, enabling it to take action if necessary (e.g., security-relevant chrome JS).
3. **Avoid Large Computations on Low Memory**: Prevent SpiderMonkey from initiating computationally expensive tasks (e.g., parsing or compiling) when memory is low.
4. **Default Crash Behavior for Unrecoverable Cases**: By default, trigger a crash when an OOM condition cannot be recovered from.

summary: Token Bucket for Network Bursts
description:
A network trace of a highly sharded site, like pinterest, shows large runs of of both SYNs and then later on GETs that are all sent simultaneously.

The ethernet/wifi driver is going to place those packets on the 'wire' as quickly as it can serialize them and when they hit the cable-modem (or equivalent) that steps down the upstream bandwidth from LAN speeds to ISP-upstream speed a queue will form. At some point we're going to overflow that queue and you can see from the linked bugs exactly that happening (packet loss requiring handshakes and requests to be resent).

By smoothing that data out a little bit (allowing a burst but bounding it, and then pacing the remainder of the flight) we ought to be able to shift the queueing into the browser and get better network behavior. I'd suggest we start by trying to subject SYNs and HTTP request headers to this.

Its worth experimenting with anyhow - I don't expect we would actually need to delay things very long in terms of pacing beacuse the problem is one of instantaneous queue size and that queue will empty fairly quickly. This should also have the symmetric (and desirable) property of smoothing out when the reply data arrives (which can also induce loss with itself).

Here is a standardized, professional description of the enhancement request:

**Request:** Implement Token Bucket for Network Burst Handling

**Objective:** To mitigate network congestion and packet loss caused by simultaneous transmission of SYNs and GET requests on highly sharded sites.

**Background:** Network traces have revealed large bursts of packets being sent concurrently, leading to queue overflows at the cable-modem level. This causes packet loss, requiring retransmissions and negatively impacting network behavior.

**Proposed Solution:** Implement a token bucket mechanism that limits burst transmission rates and paces remaining packets, shifting the queueing burden from the ISP's upstream bandwidth to the browser. Initially, focus on applying this approach to SYNs and HTTP request headers.

**Expected Benefits:**

* Improved network behavior by reducing packet loss and retransmissions
* Smoothing out instantaneous queue sizes and emptying queues quickly
* Symmetric pacing of reply data transmission upon arrival

summary: implement spdy persistent cwnd (type) setting
description:
spdy has a mechanism as part of the settings frame where a server can inform the client of some network condition about the existing session so that the client can echo it back in the future rather than starting from scratch. it does that with the PERSIST_FLAG.

This patch implements the echoing of type 5 (CWND) in connection entry session state - no state is preserved between restarts. The server can use this to more accurately size the initial sending window than a clean connection would.

Server support for this on google.com is actually broken right now (the effect is a nop), but I've been working with that team and it will be repaired at the next google.com kernel refresh (unscheduled). We can pipeline this a little bit by getting the feature in.

Our support looks just like chrome's from a packet trace point of view.

To load gmail with a full cache it takes me 40 packets of data.. with an empty cache it takes more like 400. That's plenty of data flow to feel the effects of this.

Even with the small 40 packet case a CWND change to 30 (the most common value recorded by our user's telemetry) saves a round trip time and common values I saw when testing would save two of them. So that's on average a couple hundred ms improvement.

The one concern here is that this is really another server cookie mechanism and has privacy implications. It should have a privacy review before being enabled, which I will schedule. This patch includes the feature as turned off by default (controllable by a pref) until that is sorted out. I was trying to modify our timer (TimerThread and nsTimerImpl) to use NowLoRes() when possible (for larger duration/delay values).  Not an easy task at all.

TimeStamp::Now() on windows works the way it stores both QueryPerformanceCounter AND GetTickCount values.  NowLowRes() only GetTickCount.

We always count TimeDuration as a result of two TimeStamp's difference, where usually one of them is Now() to have a meaningful value in hands to use for logic decisions.

Here is a standardized description that clearly conveys the request's main purpose and details:

**Enhancement Request: Optimized TimeStamp Arithmetic for Performance Improvement**

The goal of this enhancement is to improve performance by intelligently selecting between high-resolution (`TimeStamp::Now()`) and low-resolution (`TimeStamp::NowLoRes()`) timestamp arithmetic based on the time difference between two timestamps.

Currently, `TimeStamp::Now()` uses both QueryPerformanceCounter (QPC) and GetTickCount (GTC), resulting in slower but more accurate measurements. In contrast, `TimeStamp::NowLoRes()` relies solely on GTC, providing faster performance at the cost of lower resolution.

We propose introducing two new methods:

1. `bool TimeStamp::NowLessThan(TimeStamp& other)`: determines whether the current timestamp is less than another given timestamp.
2. `TimeDuration TimeStamp::NowMinus(TimeStamp& other)`: calculates the time duration between the current and a given timestamp.

These methods should dynamically select between `TimeStamp::Now()` and `TimeStamp::NowLoRes()` based on the time difference, using `NowLoRes()` when the difference is greater than 150ms. This approach aims to balance performance with accuracy, potentially yielding significant improvements in timer-related operations, particularly on platforms where QPC is significantly slower than GTC.

**Enhancement Request: Background Sweep for Type Objects**

To further optimize garbage collection performance, we propose sweeping type objects on the background thread. This enhancement builds upon existing work that has already swept shapes and baseshapes in the background.

However, a potential issue arises with the `TypeCompartment::markSetsUnknown()` function, which iterates over all type objects in the compartment. To mitigate this risk, we have modified the behavior to ensure that type compartment iteration is restricted while the background thread is sweeping. Specifically, when iterating over type compartments, the foreground thread will now wait for the background sweep operation to complete before proceeding.

This change ensures that no garbage collection slices occur during iteration and introduces a safety assertion in debug builds to verify this behavior. Although this may introduce occasional pauses, our analysis suggests that these occurrences are rare in practice.

The `js_DumpValue` function should provide distinct representation of positive zero (0.0) and negative zero (-0.0) in its printout. description:
Please create a certificate error reporting mechanism that will transmit and store the following information on a Mozilla server, allowing the data to be analyzed both automatically and manually.
- Domain of bad connection
- Error type (e.g. Pinning, domain mismatch, etc)
- Cert chain (at minimum, same data to distrust each cert in the chain)
- Request data (e.g. User Agent, IP, Timestamp)

Initially this reporting mechanism will be used to report, store, and analyze certificate pinning violations. In the future it could also be used for user-reported certificate errors, and other related concerns.

Certificate pinning is a mechanism by which site owners can specify a set of keys (actually fingerprints of the keys) such that in the next connection to the site, the set of keys in the certificate chain MUST intersect with the set of keys 'pinned' in the browser.
- https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=744204
- https://wiki.mozilla.org/Security/Features/CA_pinning_functionality

When the set of keys in the certificate chain do not intersect with the set of keys 'pinned' in the browsers, then an alert will be generated and sent to Mozilla to be stored and analyzed. There may be some false alarms, but if a real issue (such as MITM) is identified, the security-group should be alerted for further action.

Here's a standardized description of the enhancement request:

**SSL Error Reporting Mechanism**

We propose developing an SSL error reporting mechanism that captures and stores relevant data on a Mozilla server. This feature will facilitate both automated and manual analysis of certificate errors, enabling more effective identification and mitigation of potential security threats.

The system will collect and transmit the following information:

* Domain affected by the connection issue
* Error type (including pinning, domain mismatch, etc.)
* Certificate chain details, including any distrusted certificates
* Request data (such as User Agent, IP address, and timestamp)

Initially, this reporting mechanism will focus on detecting certificate pinning violations. However, it could be expanded to support user-reported certificate errors and other related security concerns in the future.

When an alert is generated due to a lack of intersection between pinned keys and those in the certificate chain, it will be sent to Mozilla for storage and analysis. This system will help identify potential Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) attacks or other security issues, triggering alerts for further action by the security team.

Here is a standardized description conveying the main purpose and details of the enhancement request:

**Telemetry for Server Hello Size**

We propose gathering telemetry data to monitor the size of Server Hello messages in SSL handshakes, specifically focusing on the number of bytes sent from the server before certificate verification. This information will help assess whether large certificates or intermediate chains are causing additional round trips during the handshake process.

The goal is to evaluate the effectiveness of the TLS-cached-info extension, which aims to mitigate this issue by utilizing cached information for repeated connections with the same hosts. If the data collected shows that this problem is significant, we may consider implementing support for the TLS-cached-info extension in both Mozilla and open-source projects (e.g., mod_ssl/apache).

This telemetry patch will utilize a plaintext nspr layer to track the bytes sent from the server during the handshake process, providing valuable insights into the SSL handshake performance. The data collected will inform our decision on whether to prioritize implementing this solution.

summary: Cache Effectiveness Telemetry
description:
Let's find out if the HTTP cache helps us or hurts us.

The strategy here is a little crude, but I can live with that.

The experiment takes selected aurora or nightly sessions and puts them into an "experiment mode" for 15 minutes after waiting 2 minutes after startup for things to settle down. After the 15 minutes expires things return to previous behavior.

To be selected, a session needs to have the allow-experiments pref set to true (its default), and the use-cache pref set to on (the default). Beyond that 1 in 16 sessions is selected at startup time.. so if this really screws you up you can just restart :)

If you're in the experiment you get further divided into 1 of 4 groups. Two of those groups have their cache enabled, two have it disabled. Those categories are further split into "fast connections" and "slow connections".. (fast vs slow is pretty crude, I count the number of tcp connects in those first 2 minutes that happen <=125 ms as fast and > 125ms as slow.. if you're at least 1/3 fast I say its a fast-connected-machine.. if I thought it was worth revising I would.)

Finally, assuming the experiment is running, a datapoint is collected for every http transaction measuring the elapsed time from asyncopen to the time onStopRequest is called... this is reported through telemetry along with which group you are allocated to.

The intent is we should be able to see if having the cache enabled speeds things up, slows things down, or changes the tail.. and if it has a better effect on "slow" networks than fast ones. It intentionally doesn't measure hit rate or anything like that - just the overall performance profile.

Here is a standardized description of the enhancement request:

**Cache Effectiveness Telemetry**

Objective: To investigate the impact of HTTP caching on system performance and network latency.

**Experiment Design**

The experiment randomly selects 1 in 16 sessions at startup, with the following criteria:

* The `allow-experiments` preference is set to true (default).
* The `use-cache` preference is set to on (default).

Selected sessions are divided into four groups based on cache enabled/disabled and network connection speed (fast/slow). Network speed is determined by the number of TCP connections established within the first 2 minutes, with fast connections defined as those completing connections in <=125ms.

During each HTTP transaction, telemetry data is collected, including:

* Elapsed time from asynchronous open to onStopRequest call.
* Group allocation (cache enabled/disabled and network speed).

This experiment aims to measure the overall performance profile of HTTP caching on system performance and network latency, specifically comparing its effects on fast and slow networks.

summary: Make <input type=range> usable for media controls
description:
Created attachment 729911
Screenshot of current video controls

I'd like to eventually switch Firefox's default video/audio controls to fully using HTML, instead of XUL. One part of this would be eliminating the current <xul:scale> (used for selecting the playback position), probably to a <input type=range>. This isn't currently possible because <input> isn't flexible enough. Maybe it never will be, but it seems like there's a lot of overlap and these things would generally be useful.

A few of the things I've found so far:

1) Putting a text label (showing the current time offset) in the thumb.

CSS could almost handle this:

  <input type=range currentTime="0:38">
  ::-moz-range-thumb::after {
    content: attr(currentTime);
  }

Except the CSS spec says you can only use 1 pseudoelement in a selector (but does add "Note: A future version of this specification may allow multiple pseudo-elements per selector.").


2) Allow vertical offsetting of ::-moz-range-thumb

Our video controls have a a pointy thumb that should just touch the top of the track. But -moz-range-thumb seems to force centering the thumb on the track. I can push it up, but my hacks either cause extra padding underneath the track or cause the image to be clipped at the top. (Notice in the screenshot how the thumb extends above the control bar)

    input::-moz-range-thumb {
      background: url(chrome://global/skin/media/scrubberThumb.png) top no-repeat;
      width: 33px;
      height: 28px;
    }


3) Allow ::-moz-range-thumb to overhang track

Note how the video control thumb is fairly wide. When the thumb is at the far left or right of the track, half of it should overlap. EG:

   _______                     _______
  (_00:01_)                   (_02:59_)
      v                           v
      =============================

(Alternatively allow using padding-left + padding-right on ::-moz-range-track without changing where the thumb is drawn? That seems more confusing, though.)


4) Separate styling of the track before/after the thumb.

To make the playback position even more obvious, we style the track differently to the left and to the right of the thumb. The screenshot shows this as a subtle effect; YouTube uses a bright red track to the left of the thumb. It would be nice to have ::-moz-range-track-beginning and ::-moz-range-track-end inherit style from a parent ::-moz-range-track, too?


[Additionally, the video controls current do some ugly hacks to suppress events fired by <xul:scale>, lest content see them and start relying on them. I think that's out-of-scope here, and maybe something WebComponents should deal with instead.]

summary: Add a PodOperations.h including all the Pod* methods from jsutil.h
description:
I'm seeing way too much memset and memcmp in Gecko patches I'm looking at, and it makes me sad.  A quick overview of the operations, for people who haven't seen them before:

template <class T> void PodZero(T *t):
memset(t, 0, sizeof(T))

template <class T> void PodZero(T *t, size_t nelem):
memset(t, 0, sizeof(T) * nelem)

// Should PodZero(array) zero the first element, or the entire thing?
// Given the ambiguity, force users to use PodArrayZero to clear the
// entire thing, and &array[0] to clear the first element
template <class T, size_t N> static void PodZero(T (&)[N]);          /* undefined */
template <class T, size_t N> static void PodZero(T (&)[N], size_t);  /* undefined */

template <class T, size_t N> void PodArrayZero(T (&t)[N]):
memset(t, 0, sizeof(T) * N)

template <class T> void PodAssign(T *dst, const T *src):
memcpy(dst, src, sizeof(T))

template <class T> void PodCopy(T *dst, const T *src, size_t nelem):
memcpy(dst, src, nelem * sizeof(T))

template <class T> bool PodEqual(T *one, T *two, size_t len):
len * sizeof(T) bytes at |one| are the same as the bytes at |two|

**Enhancement Request:**

**Title:** Fallback to Baseline JIT for Enormous Functions

**Description:** When dealing with extremely large functions, Ion exhibits inefficient behavior in terms of time and space usage. To address this issue, we propose implementing a fallback mechanism that switches to the baseline JIT compiler for such enormous functions. summary: Log mixed content messages from the Mixed Content Blocker to the Security Pane in the Web Console
description:
When mixed content is blocked, an error message is logged to the Security pane in the Web Console due to Bug 837351. Earlier work in Bug 737873 warns web developers about mixed content by appending a [Mixed Content] tag to mixed content resources that are loaded in the Network pane, which links to documentation about mixed content. 737873 achieves this in a hacky way, by examining network events in the webconsole code, comparing their protocol of the requested resource to that of the parent document, and modifying the logged network message if it is mixed content.

Now that we have the security pane (Bug 837351), it makes more sense to log messages about mixed content to it. We will continue to log errors for blocked mixed content, and can now log warnings about mixed content that was not blocked. We can do this directly from inside the Mixed Content Blocker, since it is now on by default.

Two open questions are:

1. Should we continue to emit the [Mixed Content] warning tag in the Network pane? On the one hand, it might give better visibility to mixed content errors. On the other, removing this would allow us to remove all of the hacky code added to the web console for this purpose.
2. Can we still provide an informative link to documentation in the warning message? This may require a custom hook in the web console code (see http://mxr.mozilla.org/mozilla-central/source/browser/devtools/webconsole/webconsole.js#1294 for the current implementation). This might be a feature that we'd like to extend to other types of security errors as well.

Here's a standardized description of the enhancement request:

**OCSP Stapling Telemetry Collection**

We propose collecting metrics on the effectiveness of OCSP stapling in preventing CA-directed OCSP (CADOCSP) lookups. The goal is to evaluate two key aspects:

1. **Stapling efficacy**: How often does OCSP stapling prevent CADOCSP lookups from occurring?
2. **Bloat and unnecessary state transfer**: When OCSP stapling is used, how frequently do we carry around stale or redundant information that doesn't contribute new state?

To gather this data, we suggest categorizing non-resumed handshakes into the following groups:

1. Handshakes with no stapled response but did not require CADOCSP.
2. Handshakes with no stapled response but required CADOCSP.
3. Handshakes with a stapled response where CADOCSP would have been triggered even without stapling (i.e., cached staple).
4. Handshakes with a stapled response where some CADOCSP is still triggered (e.g., root or intermediate certificates).
5. Other scenarios with stapled responses.

Additionally, we propose introducing metrics to track handshake sizes with and without OCSP stapled responses, such as SSL_BYTES_BEFORE_CERT_CALLBACK_WITH/WITHOUT_STAPLING. This will help us understand the impact of stapling on handshake performance.

summary: Create or update webrtc import procedure to avoid problems with history blowup
description:
The as-designed (in webrtc_update.sh) import mechanism can't be used, because it imports too much history into m-c if merged directly.  We've been doing it "by hand" after running the import process, and also (partly because of this, and partly from lack of knowledge) not been using it to hold patches-for-upstreaming as it was designed to.  (It imports from webrtc.org, processes any deletions or renames, deletes things not wanted, and then applies any to-be-upstreamed patches (by merging from a bookmark), leaving a repo set for merging to m-c -- which we can't do)

We need to revised this to work better, or find a way to replace it.  Especially we need to improve our ability to manage upstreamed patches.

See also bug 688178 and bug 818631 (and some others), and the webrtc_updates bug used to track bugs that have been proposed to upstream.

(This is similar to the issues surrounding all library imports, and the lack of standardization of how we deal with them - even the directory structure or ability for someone (or code) to recognize a directory is an import).

Right now I can do the merge by hand in a day or so (and it's gotten a bit easier since we removed all the peerconnection/jingle-related code).  There are exceptions where the merge part of the process (which has to be done in any case) is trickier because of widespread changes or renames in the upstream.  Hopefully the worst of these is done now that they converted to stdint types in this last update.

In the most recent update I did, I simply replaced media/webrtc/trunk/webrtc, then took an hg diff off all changes since the last base-code import (i.e. all our changes), and re-applied that as one patch, and dealt with the conflicts.  As mentioned, the stdint change made almost all code patches in this diff conflict, which made this merge a bear, but that shouldn't be normal.  It does lose hg blame of what patch a particular change came from, which is unfortunate but not horrible (it's still possible to see the patches applied to the file in the log).

Here is a standardized description that clearly conveys the request's main purpose and details:

**Request:** Enhance Webrtc Import Procedure for Efficient Patch Management

**Description:**

The current Webrtc import process, as implemented in webrtc_update.sh, is experiencing issues with excessive history imports into the Mozilla-central (m-c) repository. As a result, patches intended for upstreaming are not being properly applied and managed. To address this, we need to revise or replace the existing import mechanism to better handle patch management.

**Specific Requirements:**

1. Improve the ability to manage upstreamed patches
2. Enhance the Webrtc import process to minimize history imports and conflicts
3. Standardize the library import process to enable efficient patch management

**Background:**

Similar issues have been observed with other library imports, highlighting the need for standardization in how we deal with them. The current manual merge process is time-consuming and prone to errors, especially when dealing with widespread changes or renames in the upstream repository.

**Proposed Solution:**

We recommend revising the Webrtc import procedure to ensure efficient patch management and minimize the risk of conflicts. This may involve implementing new tools or processes to streamline the import and patch application workflow.

Note that I've rewritten the description to maintain clarity, conciseness, and professional language while removing direct references to original wording.

Here is a standardized description of the enhancement request:

**Feature Request: API for Overriding Page Swiping Animations**

We are considering implementing a web-based API that allows developers to disable or override page swiping animations on specific HTML elements. This would provide a way for modern websites with dynamic content, such as side-scrolling and swiping gestures, to function seamlessly across various browsers.

**Rationale:**
The introduction of bug 678392 has caused issues with some websites, particularly those that rely heavily on swipe gestures for navigation. While this feature could be valuable for certain applications, it also raises concerns about inconsistent user experiences and potential misuse by developers who may use the API out of convenience rather than necessity.

**Key Use Cases:**
Modern websites that employ side-scrolling and swiping gestures to create dynamic content would benefit from this feature. Examples include Apple's Mac Pro page (2013 version) and Google Drive's Spreadsheets, which currently disable swipe gestures in Webkit-based browsers to prevent issues.

We welcome UX feedback and discussion on the pros and cons of implementing this API to ensure it aligns with our product goals and user expectations.

    masm.jump(ifFalsy);

summary: Use immediate absolute addresses on x64 when possible
description:
On x64, code sequences like this are common:

[Codegen] movl       $0x2e6c300, %r11d
[Codegen] cmpl       $0x0, 0x0(%r11)
[Codegen] je         ((1655))

Since 64-bit addresses can't fit into 32-bit immediate fields in general, codegen just always materializes them into a register. However, it's pretty common for these absolute addresses to actually reside within the virtual address space addressable by the 32-bit immediate value. When it does, such code can be written like this:

[Codegen] cmpq       $0x0, 0x2e6c300
[Codegen] jae        ((1655))

The following patch sequence implements this, and harmonizes the x86 and x64 backends somewhat.

* Allow users to quickly enable or disable specific devices without uninstallation.
* Prevent browser hang-ups and improve overall user experience.

Reviewing the talkback documents on hal, I found that it is possible to upload files as part of the talkback submission process. I think this would be very helpful for collecting information on crashes caused by extensions and/or plugins.

It is possible to update the master.ini file for people who send in talkbacks so that we might collect data on deployed browsers that have crashed.

To start, it would be good to grab an existing extensions.rdf from the profile. This should be possible in deployed copies of browsers. Going forward, it would be good to create a summary file that would contain additional information such as installed plugins or globally installed extensions.

Here is a standardized description based on the provided enhancement request:

**Request:** Enhance Talkback Submission Process to Collect Extension and Plugin Data

**Description:**

To improve the quality of crash reports submitted through the talkback process, we propose collecting additional data related to browser extensions and plugins. This will enable more accurate identification of potential causes for crashes.

**Key Features:**

1. **Existing Extensions Data:** Retrieve an existing `extensions.rdf` file from the user's profile at the time of submission.
2. **Summary File Generation:** Create a summary file containing information on installed plugins and globally installed extensions to provide context for crash analysis.
3. **Master.ini Updates:** Update the master.ini file to collect data on deployed browsers that have crashed, including browser versions and configurations.

**Benefits:**

This enhancement will facilitate more effective troubleshooting and debugging of crashes caused by extensions and plugins, ultimately leading to improved user experience and faster resolution of issues.

Here is a standardized description of the enhancement request:

**Request to Refactor Internal MDG Structure**

The internal structure of the nsXFormsMDGNode object requires optimization. To improve efficiency and reduce redundancy, we propose consolidating shared context variables (mContext*) into a single instance data node scope, eliminating the need for duplicate storage across multiple MIP types. Additionally, the three PRBool flags should be refactored to utilize packed boolean representations (PRPackedBool) to ensure compiler compatibility and optimal memory allocation.

summary: Lithium, a testcase reduction tool (delta debugger)
description:
I wrote a testcase reduction tool that I'm calling Lithium.  I'm about to attach an alpha version to this bug.

I've already used it to reduce two Stir DOM assertions, bug 328944 and bug 328946.  This alpha should also work with other line-based fuzzers such as Random Styles, Random JS, and CSSGen.  A future version will work with other fuzzers whose output has more fragile structure (e.g. xangle, stirdom-during-mutation-events).

It's extensible to types of bugs other than assertions, hangs, and crashes.  If you want to reduce a testcase that leaks, triggers valgrind warnings, makes Firefox stop painting, or even creates a different DOM two versions of Firefox, you just have to create a program or script whose return value indicates whether the bug was triggered.

Bob Clary expressed concern that releasing this tool would make it easier for blackhats with fuzz-testing tools to create reliable exploits.  Fuzz testing is certainly not unknown outside of the Mozilla security group (see e.g. bug 328937 comment 7 and bug 264944).  On the other hand, releasing it would have some benefits: easier reductions for bug reporters and Gecko hackers outside of the security group (automated testcase reduction is useful even with non-fuzz testcases), and feedback on the tool itself.

I'm making Lithium live in this security-sensitive bug for now.  Even if we released Lithium before we release our fuzzers, this bug would remain security-sensitive because it mentions our fuzzers.

summary: Instrument detection of bad pointers and objects
description:
I would like to add the ability to detect the use of "bad pointers" and "bad objects" in debug builds in as much of the code as possible. By "bad pointer", I mean pointers that point to an invalid address such as MSVC's 0xdddddddd|0xcdcdcdcd|0xfdfdfdfd or point to an obviously bad address like 0x00000001. By "bad objects" I mean an object which has either been deleted or otherwise been "stomped on". It would also be good to have some code in release builds which also test for a more limited definition of validity and which will automatically kill the browser if the validity test fails.

The motivation behind this is the randomstyles testing I have been doing where many of the crashes are due to pointers contained in deleted objects or pointers that have somehow been initialized to a very small value. It seems to me that crashes due to these errors can lie in wait like mines which are only detonated much later when the code actually steps on them. By reporting these problems as soon as possible I think it will help locate and fix the actual errors faster|easier.

This is in addition to such such "semantic" checks (like testing if the next sibling of the last node in a linked list is null) which may fire on such bad objects|pointers but which is too late and does not clearly indicate that the error is memory related.

wish list: 

* cross platform solution (win/linux/mac) although if it is only possible in windows it would be better than nothing.

* a macro assertion (VALID_POINTER(p,m)) that will fail if p is invalid in someway.

* modifications to nsAutoPtr and nsCOMPtr to call VALID_POINTER when appropriate and perhaps allow comparisons between pointers.

* an invariant in objects which when violated means the object has been corrupted.

I think nsAutoPtr and nsCOMPtr are the easiest to start with and will cover the most code with least effort. Afterwards particular problematic classes can be instrumented on an "as needed" basis.

This is security confidential due to its relation to fuzz testing and the security implications of find such errors.

**Request for Pointer and Object Validity Detection**

We propose implementing a cross-platform solution to detect and report invalid pointers and objects in debug builds, with an option to automatically terminate the application if validity checks fail in release builds. The goal is to identify memory-related errors that can cause crashes or security vulnerabilities.

The solution should include:

1. **Pointer validation**: Implement a macro assertion (`VALID_POINTER`) that fails if a pointer points to an invalid address or has been "stomped on".
2. **Object validity checks**: Introduce invariants in objects to detect corruption, and modify `nsAutoPtr` and `nsCOMPtr` to call the `VALID_POINTER` macro when necessary.
3. **Cross-platform compatibility**: Ensure the solution works on Windows, Linux, and macOS (with a preference for cross-platform implementation if possible).

Key benefits include:

* Early detection of memory-related errors that can cause crashes or security vulnerabilities
* Improved debugging experience with clear indication of error types
* Enhanced code reliability through robust pointer and object validation

This enhancement is considered confidential due to its relation to fuzz testing and security implications.

Here is a standardized description of the enhancement request:

**Enhancement Request: Optimized Repeat State Management**

The current implementation of `UpdateRepeatState()` traverses the tree to update repeat state information. To improve performance, we propose introducing an optimization that utilizes a `isTemplate` flag returned by `nsIXFormsContexControl::getContext()`. This flag would be set on controls receiving context and propagated to child elements, eliminating the need for tree traversal.

**Key Changes:**

* Introduce a `isTemplate` bit in `nsIXFormsContexControl::getContext()` that indicates template-based repeat state.
* Set this bit permanently for Repeat and Itemset controls, as they always wrap unrolled content within context containers.
* This optimization will significantly reduce the time required to update repeat state information.

This revised description maintains the clarity and conciseness of the original request while rephrasing it in professional language.

**Request:** Implement Support for Custom Menu Font in Themes

**Description:**

To enhance theme customization, we propose introducing support for setting a custom font for menus using the `-moz-pull-down-menu` ID. Currently, themes rely on the existing `font: menu;` declaration, which applies the system font with a reduced size. However, this approach can have unintended consequences when applied to other elements.

Research suggests that the `-moz-pull-down-menu` ID aligns with the intended purpose of styling pull-down menus, as defined in the CSS3 working draft (http://www.w3.org/TR/2002/WD-css3-ui-20020802/#system0). By utilizing this ID, theme authors can specify a distinct font for menus without affecting other elements.

This enhancement would provide theme creators with more precise control over menu styling and ensure consistency with the intended CSS standard.

Using XBL to get the XForms extension going was not a bad idea, though there are long term problems with continuing with it:
1) When you disable Javascript in Firefox the XForms extension stops working.  One of the key benefits of XForms is that it doesn't (or shouldn't) require Javascript.
2) It adds a fair amount of overhead.  Writing it natively, extending using standard XPCOM/C++ mechanisms, would greatly improve efficiency not having to context switch between C++ and JS.  This will also lay the ground work for providing XForms support natively, if that day were to come.
3) Simplifies coding and debugging.  Debugging XBL is a learned skill, no debuggers exist and if using JS debugger requires reworking XBL.

summary: Option to warn user when site certificate uses intermediate certificates
description:
User-Agent:       Mozilla/5.0 (Windows; U; Windows NT 5.1; en-US; rv:1.8.1.2) Gecko/20070222 SeaMonkey/1.1.1 Mnenhy/0.7.5.0
Build Identifier: 

Users should have an option to be warned if a secure Web site uses a site certificate that was signed, not by a root certificate in the browser database, but instead by an intermediate certificate.  This option should allow the user to indicate the number of intermediate certificates allowed before the warning appears.  The warning should include buttons to allow the user to continue or cancel viewing the site.  

Reproducible: Always




I went to check a bank statement on the Web.  The bank's Web site had a site certificate that was signed by a Network Solutions intermediate certificate.  The Network Solutions certificate was signed in turn by a USERTRUST Network intermediate certificate.  The USERTRUST Network certificate was signed by an AllTrust root certificate (not by a USERTRUST Network root certificate).  

Neither the Network Solutions certificate nor the USERTRUST Network certificate are in the Mozilla database.  (The USERTRUST Network intermediate certificate is NOT one of the five root certificates in the database.)  Neither Network Solutions nor USERTRUST Network are listed by WebTrust.  

The AllTrust root certificate is in the Mozilla database.  AllTrust is part of Comodo, which has a WebTrust seal.  

AllTrust and Comodo do not control Network Solutions or USERTRUST Network.  The WebTrust seal for Comodo does not apply to Network Solutions or USERTRUST Network.  Thus, my bank's site certificate is at the end of the chain AllTrust > USERTRUST Network > Network Solutions > bank.  This creates a questionable level of trust in the bank's Web site.  

Since certificate authorities often use intermediate certificates to sign site certificates, there is a need to trust such chains at least three links in length.  However, four or more links in length might raise concerns.  The length of a chain of trust should be something the user can control.
