Here is a standardized description of the enhancement request:

**Request:** Distinction between MIME and Protocol Handlers in Handler Information Objects

**Purpose:** Enhance the current handling of `nsIHandlerInfo` objects to differentiate between those representing MIME handlers and protocol handlers, enabling more precise identification and manipulation of handler types.

**Details:**

1. **Differentiation Mechanism**: Introduce an interface (e.g., `nsIProtocolInfo`) that only protocol handlers can implement through QueryInterface (QI) operations, while allowing MIME handlers to be QIable to a different interface (e.g., `nsIMIMEInfo`).
2. **Scheme Retrieval**: Provide a way to obtain the scheme associated with a protocol handler object. This can be achieved by:
	* Adding a "scheme" property to the proposed `nsIProtocolInfo` interface.
	* Introducing a "type" property to `nsIHandlerInfo`, where it would contain the scheme for protocol handlers and the MIME type for MIME handlers.

**Additional Consideration:**
If implementing the latter approach, consider retaining the existing `nsIMIMEInfo::MIMEType` property for backwards compatibility while sharing storage with the new "type" property.

3. Did the click work ?, click again, hmmm. 

Now if you manually focus to the new Tab (I have TMP installed with "multi-line-Tabs" enabled) you would have two Tabs opened.

If clicking "Learn More" causes the Tab to be "on top" (yet under the "Add-ons Pane") you could at least see part of the information that was not obscured by the "Add-ons Pane" (thus clicking from one result to the next, and each "Learn More" to each "Learn More" for 'quick details') _WITHOUT_ actually focusing the Tab, yet having it "on Top", (yet under the "Add-ons Pane" is likely the most desirable mode of operation.

Alternately, put the newly created Tab fully "on top" (above everything, even the "Add-ons Pane") and let the user chase back to the "Add-ons Pane" if they are fickle about their quest for knowledge. I feel this is a lesser desirable mode of operation yet might be "the more expected" mode of operation (more conformist to "standard HMI", yet less helpful in this circumstance).

After clicking "Learn More" it is not obvious that your click was accepted nor is the effort of clicking rewarded in any visible manner. With Tab Mix Plus multi-row-Tabs you need to scroll down to the end of your 'tab list' to get to the newly created Tab.

summary: Include status bar / url indicator as a widget inside toolbar customization.
description:
User-Agent:       Mozilla/5.0 (Windows; U; Windows NT 6.0; en-US; rv:1.9.2.11pre) Gecko/20100925 Namoroka/3.6.11pre
Build Identifier: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows; U; Windows NT 6.0; en-US; rv:1.9.2.11pre) Gecko/20100925 Namoroka/3.6.11pre

Note: this is not about bringing back the "status bar," which has been removed, per Bug 574688.

Proposal:
1. Right click on a toolbar -> Customize...
2. Include a "Status" widget that can be added to any toolbar (including the new add-ons bar, if someone wants it at the bottom).
3. The "Status" widget would contain the following expected functionality:
-- window.status targets this field (if visible)
-- active/selected urls on a web page show up here
-- optionally, it could include historical features like the loading status of the page, like "done loading".  However, the primary purpose is showing active links.

Summary:
The lack of status/url indicator at the bottom of the window does present a usability issue for some people... and it likely going to result in many complaints.  It would be nice if we didn't have to resort to add-ons for this feature.  Considering the background this particular features has, this might be a candidate for actually including as an option in Firefox.

Usability considerations:
The status indicator has a long history.  It has DOM access (window.status) and has been used for years in all browsers.

The current move to the top of the page presents a number of usability issues for some people.  Among them include:
* visual distance -- in some cases it may be less eye movement to look down than up; this "may" cause eye strain for a small group.  I personally, have experienced this.
* noise -- the top of the window is very noisy, meaning more mental effort to process all the information in order to pick out the active/selected URL every time.  Subjectively, this makes the interface more difficult to use and/or feel less "smooth" (although most people can't describe why).
* moving target -- the active url length constantly changes it's left side based on the length of the url.  This presents another problem with mental delay as the brain has to search the space for the beginning of the URL before it can start reading it.  (Subjectively, this can give the interface a "sluggish" feel to it.)
* familiarity -- people are familiar with the old style and may prefer it.



----------
Anyways, I hope this proposal might be taken in good taste.  I know there is an add-on... but still maybe this would be worthy enough to actually keep around.  For simplicity, perhaps this new Status "widget" could be tied to the same data as the one used to show the active url in the URL bar.  That way, maybe two different code paths would not have to be maintained ... and maybe all that would be needed is the graphical widget to display and position this info into a toolbar.

Reproducible: Always

Here is a standardized description of the enhancement request:

**Feature Request:** Provide a Status/URL Indicator Widget in Toolbar Customization

**Description:** A status indicator widget will be added to the toolbar customization options, allowing users to add a "Status" widget to any toolbar, including the new add-ons bar. The widget will display the current URL, and optionally include historical features such as page loading status.

**Rationale:** The removal of the traditional status bar has led to usability issues for some users, including increased visual distance, noise, mental delay, and decreased familiarity with the interface. This feature proposal aims to address these concerns by providing a customizable widget that can be placed in a convenient location on the toolbar.

**Key Features:**

* Display current URL
* Optionally display page loading status (e.g., "done loading")
* Can be added to any toolbar, including the new add-ons bar
* Tied to the same data as the active URL in the URL bar for simplicity and code consistency

**Usability Benefits:** This feature will improve usability by reducing visual distance, noise, and mental delay, making it easier for users to access and process information. It also addresses user familiarity with the traditional status bar layout.

**Reproducibility:** This issue is reproducible in all cases, highlighting its importance as a requested feature.

*   Adding warnings about potential tracking methods beyond browser-level controls

summary: Progress throbber should differentiate between page-load progress and referenced-object-load progress
description:
I'm proposing that the progress throbber should change visually after the main document has been loaded, so that the user can see that the browser is finished loading the main document and is now loading the objects that are referenced from the document.

Suppose you have two pages loading in your browser, one which loads very slowly and one which loads quickly but references some object that loads very slowly. Looking at the progress throbber for each of these pages, you can not tell one case from the other, which is a shame, since the cases are quite different.

A typical example is a newspaper site, which in itself may be fairly responsive, containing links to external advertising servers that may be slower or even not responding at all. But sometimes the newspaper site itself may be unusually slow or not responding, and it is desirable if the progress throbber could differentiate between those cases.

Continuing the newspaper site example, suppose you have the main page loaded in your browser and you refresh the page. If the throbber doesn't stop throbbing, is that because the main document is still loading, or is it some referenced object being slow to load? You cannot really tell.

2) Load http://www.autark.se/slowpage.pl in another browser tab. This simulates the case when the main document loads slowly.
3) Compare the visual feedback from loading the two tabs.

Actual outcome:  There is no difference in the feedback.
Desired outcome: There should be a clear difference in the feedback.

Here is a standardized description:

**Request:** Update Multipart Form Upload Feature to Include Content-Length for Binary Data

**Description:** When submitting multipart/form-data requests, the content-length header is currently only set for the overall request. However, this does not provide any indication of the size of individual binary file uploads within the request. 

To improve server-side parsing efficiency and reduce processing time, it would be beneficial to include the content-length header for each binary part in multipart form uploads. This can be achieved by setting the content-length header for each sub-mime container, similar to how the overall content-length is currently set.

**Impact:** Including content-length headers for binary parts will facilitate faster server-side processing of large file uploads and reduce CPU utilization.

Here is a standardized description of the enhancement request:

**Request: Efficient Plugin Container Management**

We are requesting a feature to improve plugin container management in the browser, specifically for handling Flash content. The current implementation of plugin-container.exe has been observed to consume excessive CPU and memory resources, even when rendering simple Flash animations. This can lead to significant slowdowns in browsing performance.

To mitigate this issue, we propose implementing a mechanism that allows the user to:

1. Automatically restart the plugin container when switching between tabs with Flash content.
2. Optionally request permission to terminate running plugins like Pandora or Citrix, ensuring seamless browser operation.

Alternatively, a timed reload feature (e.g., once an hour) would be beneficial for maintaining optimal system performance.

**Key Requirements:**

* Efficient management of plugin-container.exe resources
* Automatic restart of the plugin container on tab switching with Flash content
* Optional permission request for terminating running plugins

This enhancement is expected to improve browsing performance, particularly on systems with lower-end hardware configurations.

**Request for JavaScript-Safe Quick Search Parameter**

We propose adding a new parameter (`%S` or equivalent) to support JavaScript-safe encoding of search strings in quick searches. Currently, using `%s` can lead to issues with special characters, such as double quotes, being incorrectly encoded when interpreted by the `javascript:` protocol.

To resolve this issue, we suggest introducing a new parameter that employs a more aggressive encoding scheme, suitable for JavaScript execution. This would prevent spaces from being converted to plus signs (`+`) and ensure correct handling of special characters.

Example use cases include:

* Modifying the keyword URI in `nsPlacesAutoComplete.js` to utilize the proposed `%S` parameter.
* Using the new parameter in conjunction with existing JavaScript functions, such as `unencode()`, to safely handle encoded search strings.

Here's a standardized description that clearly conveys the request's main purpose and details:

**Request:** Enhance Multi-Version Support for Firefox

**Description:**

The user experience of running multiple versions/instances of Firefox on Mac OS X is currently cumbersome, requiring manual navigation to the terminal and entry of specific flags (-profilemanager and -no-remote). This enhancement aims to simplify this process by introducing a more user-friendly approach when launching multiple instances.

**Problem Statement:** When attempting to open a second instance of Firefox, the application detects the existing instance but fails to provide a clear option for interacting with it. Instead, it displays an error message claiming that only one copy can be open at a time, which is misleading as multiple instances can indeed be launched simultaneously.

**Proposed Solution:**

Upon detecting an existing instance of a different version, the second instance of Firefox should present a dialog box offering three options:

1. Cancel: Terminates the second instance without any changes.
2. Restart with Default Profile: Relaunches the second instance with the -no-remote flag to ensure a clean profile.
3. Restart with Profile Manager: Relaunches the second instance with both -no-remote and -profilemanager flags for advanced users.

This enhancement will enhance the overall user experience, especially for web developers and beta testers who frequently work with multiple versions of Firefox.

There are likely countless add-ons that enhance this tab opening history to keep track of it all, and it is likely very complicated to implement that extensive feature into Firefox.

However, there is one way to significantly increase the usefuless of the simple behavior. Right now, after you close more tabs than that simple history keeps track of, the focus automatically returns to the right-adjacent tab. However, since new tabs also open to the right, it is more likely that the tab with focus two tabs ago is actually left-adjacent.

I would have to think that switching the choice from right/next tab to left/previous tab would be a trivial change. (However, preferences may complicate the situation: Firefox recently switched the position new tabs go, and I prefer to operate with the "switch immediately to new tab" preference turned on.)

**Feature Request:** Tab Focus Adjustment for Multiple Closed Tabs

**Description:**

When multiple tabs are closed, Firefox currently returns focus to the right-adjacent tab. However, when new tabs open to the right, it is more likely that the previous tab with focus is actually left-adjacent. To improve user experience, we propose changing the default behavior to return focus to the left-adjacent tab instead of the right-adjacent tab.

**Justification:**

This change would simplify the current behavior and align with the intuitive expectation of users. It would not require a significant overhaul of Firefox's functionality but rather a minor adjustment to accommodate user preferences.

**Request for Enhanced "Open New Window" Option**

When opening a new window in the browser, it currently defaults to loading the home group pages. However, users often desire to open a blank page instead, especially when navigating to a new website.

To provide users with more control over this behavior, we propose adding an option to the "Open New Window" feature (or Ctrl-N shortcut). This option would allow users to choose between:

* Opening their home group pages in the new window
* Opening a blank page in the new window

This enhancement aims to address user frustration and provide a more intuitive experience when opening new windows. The proposed option would be accessible through a new choice in the "Open New Window" settings, giving users the flexibility to customize their browsing experience according to their preferences.

**Reproducible:** This issue is consistently observed across all browser instances.

**Expected Resolution:** Upon implementation of this enhancement, users should have the ability to select whether they want their home group pages or a blank page opened in new windows.

summary: Allow multi-dimensional tags views
description:

Bookmark tags are great stuff because one can assign a bookmark to more categories than if using directories/folders. Using directories/folders it is
possible but one has to make copies of data. This is the strong side of tag
over folders. However if to use tags as implemented currently the creation of
flat flags structure only is possible. The tags structure can arise in one 
dimension only. Directories/folders do not show this weakness!

If to enable the tag to get other tag or more tags assigned to it will be 
possible to build up two dimensional tags structures.

Tags without any other tag/tags assigned to appear at the top-level of this 
structure. Tags with other tag/tags assigned to them appear deeper in this structure. How deep the particular tag appears depends on the tags been assigned
to it.

If to use this enhancement one no need folders any more to organize the
bookmarks.

Reproducible: Always

Steps to Reproduce:
See "details".
Actual Results:  

More tags defined.
If to show them all in the bookmarks menu, a flat structure of all tags appears.

Expected Results:  

Two dimensional structure of defined tags appears.
The tags are powerful as folders/directories are.
They are even more powerful than folders, because one can assign
an item to more categories (here tags) without doubling the object.

**Enhancement Request: Enabling Multi-Dimensional Tag Views in Bookmark Organization**

The current implementation of bookmark tags only supports flat, one-dimensional structures. This enhancement aims to enable users to assign multiple tags to a single tag, allowing for the creation of two-dimensional tag structures.

With this feature, bookmarks can be organized using a hierarchical system where top-level tags appear at the root level and sub-tags are assigned to them based on their corresponding tags. This enables users to create complex, multi-dimensional relationships between tags without needing to duplicate bookmarks or use folders.

This enhancement would eliminate the need for folders in bookmark organization, as tags could serve as both primary categorization tools and secondary assignment mechanisms. As a result, users would gain more flexibility and power in organizing their bookmarks, making them even more effective than traditional folder-based systems.

When I upgrade Firefox using Synaptic package manager, there is no warning when I extensions will be disabled for version incompatibility. While local installs of Firefox have the ability to warn the user of this (*pre*-upgrade), APT managed installs do not.

This is a major annoyance because I rely on certain extensions to make the internet not suck, and some of them are not in active maintenance. I often avoid upgrading Firefox on new minor and major version bumps because of this. Major versions bumps are especially bad because they may result in changes to datastore formats, and downgrades are not guaranteed to protect my data. The result is that I have to back up my profile before upgrade, do the upgrade, check if anything important broke, and if so, downgrade and restore.

The only tricky part here I can see here is that there *may* be multiple users with Firefox profiles on the system. An upgrade warning should *not* by default list out the extensions that each user may have new version incompatibility with on upgrade. However, I am confident that the developers can work out a solution that balances user privacy with sufficient reporting.

Here is a standardized description of the enhancement request:

**Feature Request: Restore Bookmarking Functionality**

**Request Summary:** We propose restoring key features from Mozilla and Seamonkey's bookmarking system to Firefox, specifically moving the bookmarks pull-down menu to the browser window toolbar.

**Background:** The current implementation of bookmarks in Firefox, where the pull-down menu is located on the Macintosh menu bar, can be inconvenient for users who work with multiple browser windows open simultaneously. This is particularly true for researchers and power users who require side-by-side comparison capabilities.

**Key Features to Restore:**

1. Ability to delete, file, and edit bookmarks directly from the bookmarking menu.
2. Accessibility of the bookmarks pull-down menu on the browser window toolbar.

**Benefits:** Restoring these features will improve user efficiency and productivity for those working with multiple browser windows, enabling smoother navigation and comparison of web content.

**Compatibility:** This feature is compatible with existing add-ons and patches that have restored similar functionality to Firefox 3.X. We anticipate a seamless integration with future versions of the browser.

**Request Status:** Always reproducible.

In the light of recent fraudulent SSL certificates being issued, measures should be taken to increase security of secure transactions for users. One easy and fairly unobtrusive way to do it would be as followed:

1- Firefox stores basic information about certificates of every secure site the user goes to, including the hash, expiration date, CA name and site name. Nothing should change as to what the user sees.

2- When the user goes back to that site, these information are checked. If everything is the same, nothing is shown.

The only case that would not be covered with this change would be a first visit, which would require some type of web of trust, and more user interaction on first visits, which is outside the scope of this feature request.

Note that this is a feature that should be on by default to be effective, but have a checkbox to turn on or off in the options, or in about:config.

Reproducible: Always

Nothing.

Here is a standardized description of the enhancement request:

**Request for Certificate Change Warning**

To enhance user security, we propose an optional feature in Firefox that displays warnings when a secure site's certificate has changed. This feature would monitor and compare the certificate information (hash, expiration date, CA name, and site name) of visited sites, providing alerts to users if any changes are detected.

**Key Features:**

* Stores basic certificate information for each secure site visited
* Checks this information upon subsequent visits
* Displays a warning message when a change is detected, including details on what changed (e.g., signing authority, expiration date, or site name modification)
* Warning remains visible until user interaction

**Rationale:** This feature aims to mitigate the risks associated with fraudulent SSL certificates by providing users with timely warnings about potential security threats. The feature would be enabled by default but offer an opt-out option through a checkbox in the options or `about:config`.

**Effectiveness:** This solution addresses most scenarios where fraudulent certificates are used, including state-sponsored attacks with DNS control, without significantly impacting typical user experience.

**Limitation:** First-time visits to sites would still require additional user interaction and may benefit from a separate web of trust implementation, which is outside the scope of this feature request.

summary: Add support for multiple session restore from History menu
description:
User-Agent:       Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 5.1; rv:2.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/4.0
Build Identifier: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 5.1; rv:2.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/4.0

Serious data loss issues exist in Firefox 4.0, both for people who haven't discovered the undocumented on-demand session restore - Bug 636777 - and those who have - Bug 637148, Bug 636716.

The severity of these and other related bugs could be greatly reduced by adding a basic form of multiple session restore, for instance by turning 'Restore Previous Session' on the History menu into a parent menu.  Example submenu items would be as follows:

  Session 1 (1 Window, 1 Tab, 1 Group)
  Session 2 (2 Windows, 53 Tabs, 2 Groups)

So if, in the example above, Session 1 was the instance of about:home from Bug 637148, the user could easily locate their main session, Session 2.  (The button on about:home would always restore Session 1.)

The menu would hold the last 5 or so sessions.  (Each session is just a small database of windows, tabs, tab order, favicons, etc, so has a small filesize.)  It would certainly be desirable to also have a way to delete individual sessions, but the primary issue here is of widespread data loss - potentially for tens of millions of users.  The solution here would alter that to data misplacement.

Note that selecting Session 2 in the above example would make it Session 1 - in other words, no sessions would be lost just by looking for the relevant session.  Exiting at this point would retain it as Session 1.  (By naming the session files sessionstore1.js, sessionstore2.js, etc, advanced users could delete an unwanted session with the browser closed; if sessionstore1.js was not found by Firefox on restart it would rename sessionstore2.js to 1 and so on.)

Bug 645554 suggests a way to opt out of a session restore on startup.  What would probably be more useful would be a way to escape from a session load already in progress, for instance by pressing the Escape key.  Tabs that were yet to partially load would be automatically closed, and partially loaded ones would be stopped from loading further.  Therefore, if the user had a couple of 10-tab sessions on the History menu they could quickly determine the important one, by halting it if wrong.  (Again, note that halting doesn't delete it; it would be retained as Session 1 - the most recently accessed.)

Multiple session support actually already exists in the program: It's possible to have nested instances of the about:sessionrestore tab saved, and these work correctly.  But while that sort of graphic user interface - which shows individual tab names with favicons - would be desirable, a basic submenu as above would be sufficient to avoid data loss in most cases.  Fancier solutions could be developed later.  But it's critically important to have some sort of solution _built into the browser_ (not in the form of an add-on) asap.

Reproducible: Always

Steps to Reproduce:
1. See relevant bugs.
Actual Results:  
Session is lost

Expected Results:  
Session is located

Here is a standardized description that clearly conveys the main purpose and details of the enhancement request:

**Enhancement Request: Multiple Session Restore from History Menu**

The current implementation of session restore in Firefox 4.0 has been identified as a major source of data loss for users. To mitigate this issue, we propose adding basic support for multiple session restore from the History menu.

**Key Requirements:**

* Display a list of recent sessions (e.g., last 5 sessions) with detailed information (session name, window count, tab count, group count)
* Allow users to easily locate and select their desired session
* Provide an option to delete individual sessions
* Ensure that switching between sessions does not result in data loss; instead, the new session becomes the active one, while the previous session is retained
* Consider incorporating an escape key functionality during session load to halt loading of partially loaded tabs

**Rationale:**

The primary goal of this enhancement is to significantly reduce the likelihood of data loss due to incorrect or missing session restores. This feature would be particularly beneficial for users who rely on Firefox as their primary browser, potentially affecting tens of millions of users.

**Existing Similarities and Considerations:**

* Multiple session support already exists in the program through nested instances of the about:sessionrestore tab; however, a more accessible and user-friendly solution is needed
* A basic submenu with session details would be sufficient for initial implementation, with potential for fancier solutions to be developed later

**Reproducibility:**
The issue can be consistently reproduced by following the relevant bugs.

By implementing this enhancement, we aim to provide users with a more reliable and user-friendly experience when restoring sessions, ultimately reducing the risk of data loss.

Here is a standardized description that clearly conveys the request's main purpose and details:

**Issue Description**

When the Firefox browser receives an excessive number of cookies from a website, it can become unresponsive due to the accumulation of cookie acceptance prompts. This issue occurs when the user has enabled cookie acceptance with the "always ask" setting in the Privacy preferences.

**Steps to Reproduce**

1. Enable "accept cookies" with the "keep until" dropdown set to "always ask" in the Firefox Preferences (Privacy tab).
2. Visit a website that sends an unusually large number of cookies, such as http://www.derwesten.de.

**Behavior Observed**

Upon loading the page, 75 cookie acceptance dialogs are displayed simultaneously, requiring the user to confirm each cookie individually. This can lead to an overwhelming and frustrating experience for the user.

**Proposed Solutions**

To mitigate this issue, two potential improvements are suggested:

a) Implement a "collect" feature that aggregates multiple cookie requests from the same domain into a single dialog, allowing users to accept or reject all cookies at once.
b) Introduce a delayed prompt mechanism, where subsequent cookie dialogs appear only after the user has made a decision for the initial cookie. If a default behavior is set for a domain after accepting 5 cookies, the remaining cookies can be handled accordingly.

**Reproducibility**

This issue is consistently reproducible in all cases.

**Enhancement Request: On-Demand Tab Loading Preference**

We propose exposing an "on-demand tab loading" preference under session restore preferences, allowing users to opt-in to load tabs only when needed. This feature is currently available through the `browser.sessionstore.max_concurrent_tabs=0` preference.

The new setting will be displayed as follows:

"When Firefox starts: [Show my windows and tabs from last time ▼]
                     [✓] Restore tabs on-demand"

By default, this option will be unchecked, preserving the current behavior. If space is limited in the preferences window, a blank line can be left for other options.

To implement this feature effectively, we suggest introducing a separate "restore tabs on demand" preference that bypasses the concurrent tab loading setting instead of resetting it to 0.

This enhancement aims to provide users with more control over their browsing experience. Suggestions for improving wording or alternative placement/exposure of this setting are welcome.

**Bookmark Order Management Enhancement Request**

**Description:**
The ability to automatically order bookmarks by name, date, or other criteria is available but lacks functionality for saving and persisting the ordered list. **Issue Overview:**

However, once an auto-ordered list is generated, there is no option to save or persist this order, forcing users to manually reapply the desired sorting each time they access the bookmarks menu.

**Expected Behavior:**
To address this limitation, a feature should be implemented that allows users to save and store ordered bookmark lists. This can be achieved through the addition of a "Permanently Order By" option or a dedicated "Save" button within the bookmark manager. This enhancement would ensure that automatic ordering is not only available but also persists across subsequent accesses to the bookmarks menu, facilitating easier and more logical access to bookmarked content.

**Reproduction Steps:**
1. Access the bookmark manager.
2. Select a folder with bookmarks.
3. Choose "Order by name" or another predefined criterion from the menu.
4. Attempt to save or persist the auto-ordered list for future reference.

**Impact:**
This enhancement would significantly improve the usability and efficiency of keyword-based bookmark organization, allowing users to maintain organized and easily accessible bookmark collections.

When using the new tab button, we propose that it remain stationary under the cursor until the user intentionally moves away from it. This behavior would ensure that multiple tabs can be opened without requiring frequent adjustments to the mouse position.

The new tab button currently relocates as subsequent tabs are opened, necessitating repeated re-aiming of the cursor.

2. Alternatively, the new tab button could be permanently relocated to the far right-hand side of the tab bar.

2. Open multiple new tabs using the new tab button.
3. Observe how the button relocates as each new tab is opened, requiring repeated adjustments to the mouse position.

We expect that the new tab button will remain stationary under the cursor until the user intentionally moves away from it, allowing for efficient and uninterrupted opening of multiple tabs.

When the user enters a search query containing a dot (.) in the Location bar and encounters a DNS lookup error, Firefox should automatically fall back to searching with the entered phrase instead of displaying an unhelpful error message.

This feature will provide users with a more intuitive experience when searching for web pages using non-standard addresses or keywords. The fallback behavior will be applied only once per session, preventing infinite loops in case of offline sites.

**Details:**

* Reproducibility: Always
* Steps to reproduce:
	1. Enter a search query containing a dot (.) in the Location bar.
	2. Press "Enter".
* Current behavior: Unhelpful error message is displayed.
* Desired behavior: Load the corresponding web page or display search results for the entered phrase.

**Request for Enhanced Session Backup Capability**

**Problem Statement:** Firefox's current session backup mechanism only retains one previous session, leaving users vulnerable to data loss in the event of a crash or unexpected closure. This issue can lead to significant productivity losses and frustration.

**Proposed Solution:** Introduce an option to store at least two previous sessions, allowing users to recover their work even after multiple closures or crashes. **Rationale:**

* Currently, Firefox's session backup is limited to a single session file (sessionstore.bak), which can be overwritten if another user inadvertently closes the browser or restores their own session.
* This limitation makes it difficult for users to recover lost sessions, including complex layouts and settings like those managed by Panorama.

**Expected Outcome:**

* Users will have a reliable way to recover previous sessions in case of data loss due to a crash or unexpected closure.
* This feature will enhance the overall user experience and reduce productivity losses associated with session recovery.

An increasingly common attack is to ask the user to paste something like this into their location bar:

**Feature Request**

To optimize channel switching efficiency, we propose enhancing the installer download mechanism. When transitioning between channels (e.g., from Aurora to Beta), the system should verify the presence of an existing, up-to-date installer for each channel before initiating a new download. This functionality will prevent unnecessary re-downloads and conserve bandwidth, particularly beneficial in mobile environments with limited data connectivity.

The current implementation downloads the entire installer package for each channel switch, even if a recent version already exists on the system. This results in redundant downloads, which can be frustrating and costly when working within constrained data budgets.

**Expected Behavior**

When switching between channels, the software should:

1. Identify the existing installer versions for each target channel
2. Determine whether an updated installer is required
3. Only download a new installer if necessary

By implementing this enhancement, we aim to improve user experience and reduce unnecessary bandwidth usage during channel transitions.

**Request for Review of Firefox User Interface**

We are seeking clarification on the design decisions behind the recent changes to the Firefox user interface, specifically in versions 4.0 and above. The increased screen area and removal of UI elements have led to concerns about usability and user experience.

**Key Issues:**

* Simplification of the UI may be beneficial for specific use cases (e.g., netbook users), but has resulted in a loss of essential functionality for average users.
* Removal of UI elements, such as the URL bar, may compromise ease of use.
* The motivations behind these changes appear to prioritize advertising space and cater to specific user groups, potentially at the expense of overall usability.

**Request:**

We would like to understand the underlying reasoning behind these design decisions and their intended benefits for users. Specifically, we are seeking insight into how these changes improve the user experience, beyond what is already provided by Fullscreen mode.

**Enhancement Request: Mobile Device as Software Security Token**

We propose utilizing the Firefox Sync connection between devices to enable a mobile device to serve as a software security token for desktop clients. This would allow users to leverage their sync-enabled mobile device to securely access private data, such as certificates and passwords, on their desktop browser.

**Key Features:**

* Desktop Firefox's Security Manager would be updated with UI to associate a sync-enabled mobile device as the software security token.
* Mobile Firefox would receive and authenticate association requests from the desktop client, while displaying relevant UI for users to accept or reject these requests.
* Optional recovery features would be implemented on desktop Firefox to facilitate replacement of lost devices.
* A minimal backend implementation in Sync servers and clients would support this functionality.

**Rationale:**
This enhancement aims to provide an additional layer of security and value to the mobile sync relationship, while also exploring innovative uses of the Firefox Sync technology. We understand that implementing this feature may require further development time, but believe it has potential to significantly enhance user experience and security.

summary: Implement a comprehensive way to show link targets in the location bar
description:
User-Agent:       Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64; rv:5.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/5.0
Build Identifier: Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64; rv:5.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/5.0

This is a request to get a feature akin bug 587908 right.

== Explanation:
Above mentioned bug was about levering the location bar by moving the information about the targets of hovered links from the (then) to-be-removed status bar to it.

As far as I understand, bug 541656 was instead implemented in the final Firefox 4, because some critical features weren’t implemented into the link target display in the location bar in time. I know of no other shortcomings that the chrome-like pop-up doesn’t share (e.g. that both can display a shorter part of a long URL than the status bar could)

Please elaborate further problems that have to be addressed before reintroducing the link target display in the location bar.

== Implementation
The implementation was removed from (I think) Firefox 4 Beta 12, and externalized into the add-on https://addons.mozilla.org/de/firefox/addon/link-location-bar/

Up next, my ideas on a possible implementation:

1. The truncating/shortness of the URL:
   This is a hard one, since the user has to see part of the current URL to
   understand that the arrow means “if you click, this URL changes to that URL”

   Maybe we can start with the right half, and then slowly and unobtrusively
   extend the width of the link target, until it covers the full location bar.
   we should also make URL and link location visually different
   (e.g. lighter colour to indicate that it isn’t the current status)

2. No location bar in full-screen mode:
   This is easier, and I can think of multiple solutions:
   • Show the navigation toolbar
     I don’t really like this one. The navigation toolbar is a clunky piece and
     contains many buttons, bells and whistles that can’t be clicked when the
     toolbar is shown on link hover.
   • Show the location bar alone, at the very top of the screen
     …or a bar that looks like it.
     This would be the same as the current implementation, but looking like the
     location bar, and only present in fullscreen mode. The shortness-problem
     can be avoided by making it full-width unless the mouse cursor would be in
     the area it covers, in which case it would span the half of the screen on
     which the cursor isn’t (see attachment)

== Note
As Dave Garrett pointed out in bug 541656, comment 113, I should file a new bug, since bug 587908 was invalidated by bug 541656, and these closed bugs are no place to discuss a new/extended reintroduction of a scrapped feature.

Here is a standardized description that clearly conveys the request's main purpose and details:

**Request for Enhanced Link Target Display in Location Bar**

We are seeking to implement a comprehensive solution to display link targets in the location bar, similar to the original concept proposed in bug 587908. However, due to certain features not being implemented in time, this feature was ultimately removed from Firefox 4.

To reintroduce this feature while addressing its shortcomings, we propose the following:

1. **URL Display**: Implement a solution that prevents URL truncation, such as gradually increasing the width of the link target until it covers the entire location bar.
2. **Visual Differentiation**: Provide clear visual indication between the current URL and the link target, using contrasting colors or formatting.

Additionally, we need to address the issue of displaying the location bar in full-screen mode. We propose two potential solutions:

1. **Display Location Bar Alone**: Show the location bar alone at the top of the screen, similar to the current implementation but with a full-width design that adapts to the cursor position.
2. **Alternative Solutions**: Explore alternative approaches, such as showing the navigation toolbar or modifying the location bar's appearance in full-screen mode.

This feature will enhance user experience by providing clear and concise information about link targets in the location bar.

Labelling this context menu command ‘Paste & Go’ or ‘Paste & Search’ has several problems:

**Title:** Improve Add-on Compatibility for Incremental Firefox Releases

**Description:**

We propose updating the compatibility flag for incremental Firefox releases, such as version 5 and 6, to ensure continued support for existing add-ons. Currently, many high-profile add-ons fail to function despite being compatible with previous versions due to the lack of an updated compatibility flag.

To address this issue, we suggest honoring the 4.* compatibility range up through Firefox 6, considering it equivalent to version 4.2.0 in the legacy system. This would minimize the number of broken add-ons and provide a more seamless user experience.

A potential implementation could involve displaying a prompt to users when they encounter incompatible add-ons, allowing them to opt-in to try these extensions despite potential functionality issues.

**Rationale:**

This change is essential for maintaining a smooth experience for users who rely on certain add-ons. Assuming compatibility as the default would enable Firefox developers to adopt a faster release schedule without compromising user satisfaction.

**Impact:**

Updating the compatibility flag and displaying prompts for incompatible add-ons would significantly reduce the number of broken extensions, ensuring that users can continue to use their preferred add-ons even in incremental releases.

summary: User preference to prevent cross-domain cookie-based tracking
description:
_tl;dr_
Add a preference for users to opt-out of cross-domain cookies


__The problem__
One problem of generated by cookies is cross-domain tracking.
When first loading a resource from tracking.com (example name. I don't know if the domain is actually used and I don't care) (inserted image, visiting tracking.com itself, etc.), tracking.com can set a cookie. Later requests to tracking.com will send this cookie, regardless of whether you visit tracking.com or any other site. Some website store in the cookie an identifier used to identify from which user the requests come from. Combined with the Referer (sic) HTTP header, not only tracking.com can identify a person, but also a browsing behavior in the tracking.com domain (which I consider acceptable) AND any other website embedding a tracking.com (which is an issue).
This is very well explained and visualized by http://collusion.toolness.org/

__The basic idea__
If I'm visiting a website from a particular origin, do NOT send cookies to other domains.
This has several limitations of course.

__Limitations__
* In some cases, the cookies could be useful anyways, so Firefox should not impose to not send the cookies, hence the idea of a user preference option.
* Some requests should always send cookies. iframes, for instance, since their content is very likely to depend on cookies. Not sending cookies could break the browing experience.
* I don't know what to think of cross-domain XHR.

__Technical details__
* If not sending the Cookie header to a tracking domain, this one is likely to send the cookie again. I think that the best thing is to ignore this new cookie and keep the previous one.
* Same-origin cookies should NOT be affected by this bug.

__How could the preference be presented to the user?__
I see two ways to set the preference.
* Block all cross-domain cookies except a user-provided white list
* Block no cross-domain cookies except a user-provided black list (default and empty black list by default for the sake of not breaking the web)
Both approaches could be provided to the user.

One good thing later down the road would be to allow users sharing their lists.
Maybe following the model used in AdBlock?
Maybe through a Sync-like mechanism?

With such a user preference, users will have a way to protect themselves from tracking. Something I hope more efficient than the Do-Not-Track header which is respected at the discretion of the server.

_Warning_
Fixing this bug may affect worldwide economy

Here's a standardized description that clearly conveys the request's main purpose and details:

**Request for Cross-Domain Cookie Blocking Preference**

Users are requesting a feature to block cross-domain cookie-based tracking, which allows websites to track user browsing behavior across multiple domains. This preference would prevent third-party cookies from being sent to other domains, enhancing user privacy.

**Rationale:**

The current implementation of cookies can lead to cross-domain tracking, where a website sets a cookie that is then sent with requests to other sites, enabling tracking and potentially compromising user anonymity. Users seek control over their browsing experience and the ability to opt-out of such tracking mechanisms.

**Requirements:**

1. Implement a user preference to block cross-domain cookies.
2. Provide two options for presenting this preference:
	* Block all cross-domain cookies except those on a user-provided whitelist.
	* Block no cross-domain cookies except those on a user-provided blacklist (defaulting to an empty list).
3. Consider allowing users to share their lists through a Sync-like mechanism or a system similar to AdBlock.

**Technical Notes:**

1. Cookies set by the same origin should not be affected by this feature.
2. When a tracking domain attempts to send a cookie, it is recommended to ignore the new cookie and maintain the existing one.

By implementing this preference, users will have more control over their browsing experience and can better protect themselves from unwanted tracking.

summary: Notify user about ToS/PP changes through the Sync client UI (Terms of Service, Privacy Policy, notification, updates)
description:
When Terms of Service or Privacy Policy are updated, the new version goes into effect without requiring every time an explicit re-agreement from the user:

TOS: “Your continued use of the Services after the effective date of such changes constitutes your acceptance of such changes.”

PP: “Mozilla may change this Privacy Policy from time to time. Each time you use the Firefox Sync Service the current version of this Privacy Policy will apply. Any and all changes will be reflected on this page. You should periodically check this page for any changes to the current policy. To make your review more convenient, we will post an effective date at the top of this page.”


Unlike many websites’ TOS, there is some promise of notification:

TOS ( https://services.mozilla.com/tos/ ) says: “If the changes are substantive, we will announce the update through Mozilla’s usual channels for such announcements such as blog posts and forums.”

PP ( https://services.mozilla.com/privacy-policy/ ) says: “Material changes will also be announced through the standard mechanisms through which Mozilla communicates with the Mozilla community.”


However, most users probably don’t read Mozilla blogs and forums. Most users won’t check for policy updates even if they care about them, because manual checking is inconvenient. Firefox Sync has the advantage of being able to have some data about the user’s usage of it, so it can have an idea on whether the user should be notified about a policy update.
For example, the client could
* tell the user if there’s been a recent update (e.g. during the last n contacts with the server).
* let the user tell it if the user wants to be notified of a certain update (e.g. store the date of the last user-acknowledged update in the User Data).

summary: Add UI for max_concurrent_tabs=0 and possibly make it the default
description:
Hello,

See discussion here : bug 561149.

In reply to Philipp von Weitershausen [:philikon] from bug 561149, comment 2

> > Does BarTab use other tricks ?
> 
> Yes. It actually prevents tabs that aren't needed from being loaded. When
> the nsISessionStore service restores tabs, BarTab will let it restore the
> browser object and the attached history, but not load the page itself. You
> can configure it to do the same when you open a link in a new background
> tab. The loading will eventually take place when you visit the tab (though
> other mechanisms would surely work). The initial idea was to reduce the
> number of CPU cycles for browser (re)starts, but it turned out it also helps
> with memory (ok, not too surprising I guess).
> 
> Some BarTab users have also reported other interesting usability side
> effects:
> 
> * A video or audio site won't start playing annoying sounds through your
> speakers when you (re)start the browser. I'm looking at you, YouTube...
> 
> * Some WiFi hotspots redirect all your website accesses to a login page,
> until you have logged in. In such circumstances, starting a browser with X
> number of tabs to restore will yield of you X copies of the login page --
> not fun. With BarTab you'll only get one.

That is interesting.

Here is my typical use of my different Web browsers :

I use to have many windows with many tabs open. Sometimes, a crash. Or a clean quitting. When I re-open the browser, all the pages load. If they load cascaded, this is a bit better, but still, 54 tabs with Flash and videos and music and ads and stuff load. That bloats the memory. And if I were still a poor victim of USB DSL modem connected to Windows PC, that would crash the computer — happily, time has changed. Other annoyance : all the music videos start at the same time, playing a cacophony. I have to, one by one, pause them and put them back at their start. Other annoyance : if the crash occurred because of too many pages loaded in memory or because of some particular page loaded, then the crash will likely re-occur.

So, what do I do ?

When I relaunch my browser, I cut the network connection : turn off Airport or unplug the network cable. So, instead of 54 heavy loaded pages, I have 54 light "Server unreachable" tabs. Happily, their address and history are saved, and they remain saved if there is again a relaunch because of a new crash or clean quitting. When I have put back the network connection, I come across some "Server unreachable" page, I load it, I read it, I come across a second one, I load it, und so weiter.

This satisfies me, except in one situation :
I had many tabs open, as usual. A crash occurred. I cut the network and I relanched Firefox. All the tabs got restored, but the pages did not load ; instead, the tabs contained "Server unreachable". But in one tab, I had written in a form, like Wikipedia editing. Normally, in this case, the new form data saving feature in Firefox rocks and restores the form with each and every comma. Perhaps the form data restoring feature shoud have kicked in, even without network, thanks to the cache. Web browsers now have cache bigger than ever, but have forgotten how to display a recently viewed page when network is down. They did that commonly 10 years ago. Nowadays, when network is off, Web browsers are lost, Safari the worst. Browsers are strange. Anyway, form data restoring feature did not kick in, and I had "Server unreachable". I put the network back, and I clicked "Retry" : the page loaded, without the stuff I had written in the form. Too bad.

So I propose the following behaviour, as an option at least, when I relaunch Firefox after a crash or a clean quitting :
All the tabs get restored, with their address and history, but they don't load. Instead, they contain the message "This tab was restored from the previous session. It is ready to load." and a "Load" button. The address, instead of "http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=djV11Xbc914", is "ready-to-load:http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=djV11Xbc914". When I click "Load", the address becomes "http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=djV11Xbc914" and the tab loads. As it loads in the current session restore feature. Not fresher. With the same use of the cache. And if I had written stuff in the form, the stuff gets restored. :-) And of course, if a restored tab is still in ready-to-load state, because I have not clicked yet on "Load", and quitting — clean or crash — occurs, then, after relaunch, it will get restored in the same state, with its address and history.

Many thanks,

Nicolas

Here's a standardized description of the enhancement request:

**Request:** Introduce UI for Handling Maximum Concurrent Tabs (max_concurrent_tabs=0) as Default Behavior

**Description:**

To improve user experience when handling large numbers of tabs, we propose implementing a feature that allows users to configure Firefox to restore tabs without loading their content upon browser restart. When the maximum concurrent tabs setting is set to 0, or possibly made the default, restored tabs would display a message indicating they are ready to load, along with a "Load" button.

Upon clicking the "Load" button, the tab's address would be updated to its original form, and the content would load as normal. This behavior would utilize the cache to restore any previously entered data, such as form information, ensuring that users do not lose their work in case of a browser crash or clean quit.

This feature would provide several benefits, including:

* Reduced memory usage by preventing unnecessary page loading
* Improved usability for heavy tab users who frequently experience crashes or clean quits
* Enhanced security by preventing potential issues with Flash and video content playing simultaneously

We suggest this feature as an optional setting to allow users to customize their experience and improve overall performance.

summary: method to allow user to grant more (or perhaps unlimited) storage for web applications
description:
User Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 6.1; WOW64) AppleWebKit/535.1 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/13.0.782.112 Safari/535.1

Steps to reproduce:

I am a web developer, with applications that will require more persistent storage than is currently offered by many web browsers:
http://dev-test.nemikor.com/web-storage/support-test/

My web applications may need to store (and later retrieve) a single string that is several megabytes long. They may also need to store multiple strings that cumulatively occupy hundreds of megabytes.


Actual results:

My current experience is that most browsers fail to provide unlimited persistent storage (localStorage, indexedDB, webSQL, etc) to web applications. Safari (and Mobile Safari) seems to be the only browser that will ask the user if they will allow more space to be used by a web application (and it is buggy). Other browsers will just throw a storage exception when the limit is reached.


Expected results:

When an asynchronous storage request is invoked in JavaScript, and the request would exceed the current storage quota, the user should be asked for permission to increase the storage permissions for the current web application. If they accept, then the asynchronous storage request should continue to execute as normal, if not then an exception should be thrown.

There is a related issue being discussed here:
https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=658117

There is a related issue being discussed in the Chromium project (Google Chrome):
http://code.google.com/p/chromium/issues/detail?id=61676

Here is a standardized description that clearly conveys the request's main purpose and details:

**Request for Enhanced Storage Permissions**

The web application requires the ability to dynamically grant more storage space to users, enabling web applications to store large amounts of data (e.g., multiple strings cumulatively occupying hundreds of megabytes) without encountering storage limitations.

Current behavior varies across browsers: while Safari prompts users to increase storage permissions, other browsers (including Chrome and Mozilla Firefox) throw storage exceptions when limits are reached. This request seeks to implement a consistent user consent mechanism, whereby the browser notifies the user if an asynchronous storage request exceeds the current quota, and allows them to opt-in to increased storage permissions.

This enhancement aligns with existing discussions in [bugzilla.mozilla.org](https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=658117) and [chromium project](http://code.google.com/p/chromium/issues/detail?id=61676), aiming to provide a consistent user experience across browsers for web applications requiring extensive storage capabilities.

**Description:** To improve security and user control, we propose adding a feature that prompts users to confirm before opening arbitrary web pages initiated by add-ons. When an add-on attempts to open a new webpage, Firefox should display a dialog box with the following options:

I am missing an option to specify the installed language. Yes, we allow the user to choose language from the website, but users tend to miss it because it is not visible enough and in order to change the language they are sent to a page with a huge list of operating systems and languages (all.html).

I'd suggest giving the user the ability to change the language of the installed product from the installer itself. Following is a user scenario which I've seen already few times in user support forums:

a. User is located in France but actually is not a fluent French speaker. 
b. User go to mozilla.com in order to download Firefox, redirected to mozilla.org/fr because of geolocation or other parameters, and is greeted by a big green download button.
c. User is not spend time reading the whole page and tiny texts and click on the download button. 
d. User is seeing French texts on the installer, but continue the installation because he thinks that he'd get the opportunity to change UI language right after the installation would complete. 
e. User is launching the application on the first time and seeking for option to change UI language. 
f. Before user gives up, he searches for answer in search engine or go to support forums and asks for help.
g. User understand he should re-download the application, which makes him anger, and he afraid to lose his browser history. 


The situation is even worse in locations were there is more than one language in major use such as Belgium for example. 


I know that the list of languages is very long and it won't be the best to let the user chose language, but here is my suggestion:

• The website links to stub installers for each locale.
• The stub installer allows the user to chose installation folder etc., and there is a dropdown list allowing the user to change installed language.
• Language chooser defaults to the language the user chose from the website ("default language"), and contain list of the most common languages for that region (see below) and by default will be the same as the stub language.
• Language parameter is sent in the full installation download URL, so even if the stub installer is in French, it might install an English application. 


As for 'list of common languages for a region', we can use the metrics data to determine which languages are the most 5 common for a region, and make it possible to override the list in order to promote new locales or better defaults. The last item in the list should be 'Other languages' which will link the user how to obtain these binaries.

Here is a standardized description of the enhancement request:

**Request:** Enhance Stub Installer Language Selection

**Description:**

The current stub installer does not provide an option for users to select the language of the installed product. This can lead to user frustration and inconvenience, particularly in regions with multiple languages in use.

To address this issue, we propose enhancing the stub installer to include a dropdown list allowing users to choose their preferred language from a selection of supported options. The language chooser should default to the language selected on the website and include a list of common languages for the user's region. This will enable users to install the product in their preferred language without having to re-download the application.

**Key Features:**

* Allow users to select installation folder and choose installed language from a dropdown list
* Default language should be the same as the stub installer language, with options for common languages in the user's region
* Send language parameter in full installation download URL, enabling selection of different languages even if the stub installer is in a specific language

**Benefits:**

This enhancement will improve the overall user experience by providing a seamless and convenient way to install products in their preferred language. It will also reduce support queries related to language selection issues.

**Notes:**

* The list of common languages for a region can be determined using metrics data, with an option to override this list to promote new locales or better defaults.
* The "Other languages" option should link users to instructions on obtaining these binaries.

To improve the user experience during migration, we need to introduce friendly names for profile selection. Currently, the migration code passes a directory name as a pseudo-identifier, which may not be descriptive or user-friendly.

* Default
* Profile 2
* Profile 3
...

The ability for Firefox to create partial thumbnails has potential benefits in features such as New Tab Page.  Currently, thumbnails are generated by taking a snapshot of a page's full width and showing a portion of the page's height.  This produces thumbnails that look like small versions of the full pages themselves.

However, showing only the top left portion of the page may make thumbnails more recognizable overall.  Attached are thumbnails as they are being displayed now in New Tab Page (left column), how they could look taking 2/3 of the page width (middle column), and how they could look with 1/3 of the page width (right column). For instance, some pages with strong branding in the upper left may be more easy to recognize, while others with more unusual orientations may be harder to recognize (such as Wikipedia).

**Feature Enhancement Request: Partial Page Thumbnails**

The Firefox browser will generate thumbnails by only rendering the top 25% of a webpage's width, rather than its full width. This design change aims to improve thumbnail recognizability and usability in features like the New Tab Page.

**Background Context**
Currently, thumbnails are created by capturing the entire page height but only a portion of the page width. However, showcasing only the top-left section of the page may enhance overall recognition of web pages.

**Objectives**

1. Investigate the impact of partial page thumbnails on page recognizability.
2. Determine whether reducing the page width affects the effectiveness of strong branding and unusual page orientations.

This enhancement request proposes testing different thumbnail widths using experimental methods such as Test Pilot or Mechanical Turk, without blocking the release of New Tab in its current form.

summary: Add digest-auth support to firefox sync client
description:
Created attachment 577486
patch adding digest-auth support

This is an experimental patch to add support for Digest-Auth as per RFC 2617, allowing it to co-exist with the existing support for Basic-Auth.  The highlights:

1) pulled all the Authenticator implementations out into a new file "authn.js"

2) added an onChallenge method to Authenticator objects.  This gives them a chance to parse the WWW-Authenticate header from 401 responses, and possibly retry the request with updated credentials.

3) added a DigestAuthenticator which implements the digest-auth protocol.

4) added a MultiAuthenticator which uses the best protocol supported by the server.

MultiAuthenticator is the key to making this work in a sensible fashion.  It first sends a completely unauthenticated request to the server, then looks at the WWW-Authenticate header in the response to find what auth schemes are supported.  It can ten select the best scheme for future use, i.e. digest if available or basic otherwise.

Thoughts?

(I briefly investigated an implementation on top of the native nsHttpDigestAuth class and its friends, but it wasn't clear how this would mesh with the existing authenticators setup.)

**Issue Description**

The default value for `browser.sessionstore.max_resumed_crashes` should be set to 0. This would prevent Firefox from automatically reloading multiple tabs after a power failure or crash, which can lead to unintended consequences such as account blocking due to excessive simultaneous hits on a website.

This behavior can lead to issues such as account blocking and requires users to manually disable the "resume from crash" option in `about:config`.

**Expected Behavior**

It is expected that Firefox should prompt the user to reload all tabs after a power failure or crash, allowing them to take control of the recovery process. This would also involve making the "resume from crash" option more accessible and user-friendly by integrating it into the options dialog.

**Proposed Solution**

Setting `browser.sessionstore.max_resumed_crashes` to 0 as the default value would help prevent unintended consequences after a power failure or crash, and provide users with a more intuitive experience when recovering their browsing session.

**Proposal: Selective Rendering for Memory Efficiency**

To optimize memory usage, we propose implementing selective rendering in Gecko. This technique would render only the visible portion of the page based on screen height (or up to 2-3 times the screen height when scrolled), reducing the need to load and maintain unnecessary content in memory.

Specifically, this approach would:

* Limit rendering to the currently visible page section
* Cache unrendered images in compressed form, decompressing only when necessary
* Unrender off-screen images to conserve memory upon scrolling

This behavior is already demonstrated by WebKit on mobile devices (e.g., iPhones), where GPU acceleration enables efficient selective rendering. We can leverage this existing technology to implement a similar solution for Firefox.

To balance performance and power consumption, we suggest offering an optional toggle controlled by a user preference (checkbox) that allows users with sufficient resources to disable selective rendering if needed.

summary: Ideas about history and tab clutter
description:
History is still linear and hasn't followed the tab-browsing age. When browsing
with multiple tabs, which site led to what (the browsing-flow) is more relevant
than the order in which they were opened that the history window shows. There is
an other kind of history, linked to the back/forward buttons, which is specific
to each tab, and empty when the tab is new.

In both cases, this feels wrong to me: the history window is almost unusable but
for the "search" feature, and going forward and backward should'nt be impaired
so much by the way in which I opened the link.

Moreover, the "open link in new tab" feature is often used as just a way to more
easily go back (to a search to get back more results for example). Or more
generally to keep some easy reference to a page you know you'll need again soon.
This, at least in my case, leads quickly to tab clutter that make finding the
right tab more difficult. This is multiplied by the number of independent tasks
you do in the same browser window, each leading to a whole tree of tabs.

People are concerned about the tab clutter problem, but none of the proposed
solutions have really cut it yet:

- The tab grouping window is nice, but requires too much manual work in my
  opinion. If I'm too lazy to have orderly tabs as I go, I probably am to sort
  them this way too. Plus, other groups feel "hidden" a little bit too far away
  to me (but that could be improved). Grouping should be done mostly
  automatically.

- An interesting extension that I find very useful (despite the way it is
  written...) is Tree Style Tab. The idea is simple, you can get a simple
  hierarchy in your tabs by making a distinction between real new tabs and ones
  opened from links. This at least groups my concurrent topics in an easily
  accessible way. But even then, the back/forward history is tab specific and
  the parent/child relationship gets a bit weird when I follow a link in the
  parent tab or even close it.


Well, the reality of it is that the browsing history is a forest. It was a tree
before tabs made their way in, but even then the multiple futures weren't
properly handled (going back then forward another way), which I have always
found mildly annoying. With tabs, you work around it by opening in new tabs in
advance; we got used to this but, because this is the only way provided. Tabs,
on the other hand, with the history seen as a forest, may be seen as only a few
highlighted items in the history: any relationship between them is still present
and could be used for a clever way to visualise or to handle some operations
(like "back").

Of course, I am not suggesting we explain to users that their history is a
forest with a new tree planted every time they click on "new tab". But merging
history and tabs in some way and finding a good way to visualise the result is
the way to go. I have a few ideas about how to do this and am starting to work
on an extension to see how usable it turns out to be (it's my first, so please
be patient while I learn XUL).



Disclaimer: I am writing this based on my personal experience. I know for a fact
that I often don't use the tools the way most people do; my goal is to make the
experience better for everyone, not just myself, so I am counting on other
user's experiences to get usable UI and features. Please tell me if I am wrong
in my assumptions about how the tabs are used, or if my ideas would make it
worse for you. I sure don't expect to get it right without lots of reviews from
different users, but I am confident this is still the way to go.

As well, a lot of people will look at a page of links and open a bunch of them in the background one after the other, planning to go through them each one-by-one. Currently, if they're all HTML5 videos, they'd each start playing at the same time.

This is why the optional setting to require user intervention is an important feature.

Here is a standardized description of the enhancement request:

**Feature Request: Domain-Specific Cookie Blocking Enhancement**

The Firefox cookie manager currently lacks the ability to effectively block cookies for entire domains. When attempting to block all cookies from a specific domain using the "Permissions" tab, it allows cookies to persist even after deletion and blocking settings are applied.

**Problem Reproduction Steps:**

1. Visit a website with multiple subdomains (e.g., www.microsoft.com).
2. Delete existing cookies.
3. Navigate to the "Permissions" tab and select the option to block all cookies from the specified domain.
4. Close the browser and revisit the website; cookies will reappear.

**Current Limitations:**

The Firefox cookie manager does not allow users to block cookies for subdomains, only for the exact domain in the URL bar. This limitation prevents effective blocking of cookies from domains with multiple subdomains (e.g., "microsoft.com" cannot be blocked if it redirects to "www.microsoft.com").

**Desired Enhancement:**

Implement a feature that enables users to block cookies for entire domains, including subdomains, and provides a more robust cookie management experience. This would align Firefox's functionality with other browsers, such as Seamonkey, which offers a more comprehensive cookie blocking mechanism.

**Rationale:**

This enhancement request seeks to address a critical limitation in the current cookie manager implementation, providing users with greater control over their online privacy and security. By allowing domain-specific cookie blocking, users can better protect themselves from tracking and data collection attempts by websites.

The new tab loading behavior should be extended to load tabs in the background during idle periods after startup, rather than only when tabs are actively accessed. This will reduce both initial startup delays and subsequent tab navigation delays.

description:
The W3C tracking preference expression (TPE) draft standard is pretty stable in a few areas, and we should start thinking about implementing the part that lets users consent to tracking (see URL field for this bug).

Right now, the UI is a checkbox and either the DNT header is not sent (checkbox off) or "DNT: 1" is sent (checkbox on).  The TPE draft defines a third state, where "DNT: 0" is sent -- a state that means the user consents to tracking. We should implement a UI and a little pref tweak to allow users to voice not only disdain for tracking via the DNT header, but also consent.

There are three parts to this change: 
1.  (UI) around a three-state thing (no comment, track me, don't track me)
2.  (pref) to store which preference the user has when they've made a choice
3.  (netwerk) tweaks -- back-end to support sending multiple values in the DNT header

Most of the work is in the UI and pref parts, and only a little in netwerk.

**Implementation Request: Enhanced Tracking Preference Expression (TPE) Support**

The goal of this implementation is to enhance the user interface for managing tracking preferences to align with the W3C TPE draft standard. Specifically, we aim to introduce a three-state UI that allows users to:

* Opt-out of tracking via "Do Not Track" (DNT: 1)
* Consent to tracking by explicitly selecting an option
* Decline to state their preference

To achieve this, we need to implement the following components:

1. **User Interface (UI)**: Develop a three-state UI with clear labels and options for users to select their preferred tracking behavior.
2. **Preferences (pref) Management**: Create a mechanism to store the user's chosen preference and provide a way to persist this choice across sessions.
3. **Network (netwerk) Tweaks**: Modify the backend to support sending multiple values in the DNT header, enabling the new three-state tracking preference expression.

This enhancement will improve the user experience by providing users with more control over their tracking preferences and aligning our implementation with industry-standard practices.

* The process is simplified, reducing the risk of introducing additional errors or overwriting user preferences.
* Non-power users will appreciate the ease of use and reduced complexity compared to the existing reset profile option.

summary: Provide the remainder of the old BarTab functionality
description:
Current versions of Firefox have the ability to either delay loading of saved tabs until the tab is switched to, or load only a few tabs at a time ("cascaded session restore"). When the first versions of this feature was first announced, it was referred to as a "built-in BarTab":
http://zpao.com/posts/cascaded-session-restore-a-hidden-bonus/

However, BarTab also included a variety of other behaviors, some of which are not present in any version of Firefox I have observed. Their absence is a major usability limitation for people who had gotten used to them in BarTab, and to the best of my awareness, there is no adequate replacement for them (via add-on or any other means) in any Firefox version.

These behaviors include:

* A clear visual indication of which tabs are loaded and which are not. (Done in BarTab by dimming, or perhaps partly graying out, the tab title and favicon.)

* The ability to manually unload tabs - or more generally, to control which tabs are and are not loaded at any given time. (Done in BarTab by "Unload Tab" and "Unload Other Tabs" context-menu entries, when right-clicking on a tab.)

* The option to switch to the nearest unloaded tab (if any exist in the current window), rather than to an immediately adjacent tab, when the current tab is closed.

For those who use them, these behaviors can be just as core to the usefulness of BarTab as the delayed-tab-loading feature itself, and having only that one feature without these others feels generally crippled. Speaking for myself (and for at least one of my siblings, who is currently raging over the UI changes resulting from a forced, unnaounced upgrade to Firefox 12), the absence of these behaviors is the major thing pinning me to Firefox 3.x.

As the cancellation of BarTab - and hence the fact that these features are no longer available from that source - is due to the incorporation of the delayed-tab-loading feature into Firefox, it seems reasonable to request that these features be likewise so incorporated.

Please restore this lost functionality.

(If it would be appropriate to file one bug for each of these behaviors, rather than tracking them all under the single request, I would be willing to do so. I have requested them all in one place because they *are* in fact tied together, by virtue of being former BarTab functionality.)
